The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Average Annual Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual average temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis using the following steps: All daily low temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average low temperature value. All daily high temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average high temperature value. Average annual temperature was calculated by taking the mean of the average daily temperature over a given year. Average daily temperature was calculated by dividing the sum of daily low temperature and daily high temperature by 2. The average annual temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average temperature. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual average temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

description: Life expectancy at birth is derived from male and female life expectancy at birth and compiled by the World Bank from sources such as (1) UN Population Division: World Population Prospects; (2) Census reports and other statistical publications from national statistical offices; (3) Eurostat: Demographic Statistics; (4) UN Statistical Division: Population and Vital Statistics Report (various years); (5) U.S. Census Bureau: International Database; and (6) Secretariat of the Pacific Community: Statistics and Demography. It is the average number of years a newborn is expected to live if mortality patterns at the time of its birth remain constant in the future. It reflects the overall mortality level of a population and summarizes the mortality pattern that prevails across all age groups in a given year. It is calculated in a period life table, which provides a snapshot of a population's mortality pattern at a given time. It therefore does not reflect the mortality pattern that a person actually experiences during his or her life, which can be calculated in a cohort life table. High mortality in young age groups significantly lowers the life expectancy at birth. But if a person survives his or her childhood of high mortality, he or she may live much longer. For example, in a population with a life expectancy at birth of 50, there may be few people dying at age 50. The life expectancy at birth may be low due to high childhood mortality, so that once a person survives his or her childhood, he or she may live much longer than 50 years. The Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual heating degree days (HDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. description: ### Overview Groundwater table decline measures the average decline of the groundwater table as the average change for the period of study (1990-2014). The result is expressed in centimeters per year (cm/yr). Higher values indicate higher levels of unsustainable groundwater withdrawals. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low risk of decline (<0 cm/yr) to extremely high risk of decline (>8cm/yr). Values are available per aquifer as defined by the [World-wide Hydrogeological Mapping and Assessment Programme (WHYMAP)](https://www.whymap.org/whymap/EN/Home/whymap_node.html). ### Methodology Aqueduct used the global hydrological model, PCRaster Global Water Balance (PCR-GLOBWB 2), to calculate five indicators. Groundwater table decline is one of those indicators and was calculated by coupling PCR-GLOBWB 2 with MODFLOW to account for lateral groundwater flow processes. This indicator used gridded 14 years of monthly groundwater heads between January 1990 and December 2014. In mountainous areas, very deep groundwater influences the averages in mountainous cells and is not representative. These cells were therefore discarded from the calculations following the method in [de Graaf et al. (2015)](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-19-823-2015). After masking the mountainous areas, the results were aggregated to groundwater aquifers derived from the [WHYMAP data set (BGR and UNESCO 2018)](https://www.whymap.org/whymap/EN/Home/whymap_node.html). Next, the monthly results were fit with first-order regression. The slope of this regression line (cm/yr) indicates the existence of a downward (or upward) trend. The trend was assessed using the coefficient of determination (R-squared) and the p value. If R-squared was greater than or equal to 0.9 and the p value was less than or equal to 0.05, the trend was accepted. Finally, raw groundwater table decline values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw groundwater table decline values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds. - Low (0-1): < 0 cm/yr - Low to medium (1-2): 0 - 2 cm/y - Medium to high (2-3): 2 - 8 cm/yr - High (3-4): 4 - 8cm/yr - Extremely high (4-5): > 8 cm/yr For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

### Overview The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average total precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the total precipitation in 2000 is actually an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Cumulative average precipitation is divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset provides projections on how precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Precipitation changes are projected to be more varied across the world, generally showing increases in mean precipitation in high-latitude regions and a pole-ward shift of subtropical arid regions. In addition, precipitation is projected to occur in fewer, but more intense events. Except in the few areas that are projected to see substantial drying, historically extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. Even as precipitation increases, dry periods are projected to increase in length and frequency. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. description: ### Overview The Urban Population dataset shows the number of people living in urban areas, expressed as a percentage of the total national population. Urban areas were determined by national statistics offices in each country and no universal definition is used to describe what constitutes an urban area. The dataset is presented at a national resolution for each year between 1960 and present. Urban growth is closely related to the three dimensions of sustainable development: social, economic, and environmental. Well-managed urbanization, informed by an understanding of population trends over the long run, can help to maximize the benefits of high levels of density while minimizing environmental degradation and other potential adverse impacts of a growing number of city dwellers. In principle, cities offer a more favorable setting for the resolution of social and environmental problems than rural areas. Cities generate jobs and income, and deliver education, health care and other services. Cities also present opportunities for social mobilization and women's empowerment. This dataset provides the basis for understanding these trends in urbanization and gives background for governments to implement policies related to these changes. This dataset was released by the United Nations Population Division (UNPD) and distributed by the World Bank Group. The Urban Population dataset is a part of World Development Indicators (WDI), the Work Bank’s primary collection of development indicators, compiled from officially recognized international sources. It presents the most current and accurate global development data available, and includes national, regional and global estimates. ### Methodology Urban population was determined by using World Bank Group population estimates and urban ratios from the UN World Urbanization Prospects. Urban ratios were created with data largely from national censuses and population registers, which typically supplied complete counts of both the total population in a country and the total population living in urban areas. The urban ratio is defined by the ratio of the total population that lives in urban areas compared to rural areas. This was combined with national population estimates to determine the percentage of the total population living in urban areas. In some cases, census data was not available for every year. In order to create yearly estimates, interpolation or extrapolation based on the data available was used. The urban population estimates used to create the urban ratio were based on the definitions used for statistical purposes by the countries and areas themselves. No universal definition for urban was used. Depending on the country, any combination of the following characteristics may have been used to distinguish urban and rural areas: information about administrative designations, population size or density, demographics, economic characteristics, and functional characteristics (existence of paved streets, water supply systems, etc.). No independent adjustment of national statistics were undertaken unless it was clear that the definitions used by a given country had changed over time in ways that would have led to inconsistencies. Despite efforts to avoid inconsistencies within countries, it was not always possible to adjust the available data in ways that ensured consistency. In some cases, inconsistencies remained because the data needed to make the necessary adjustments were lacking. In cases where adjustment was possible, every effort was made to adjust earlier data so that they conformed to the most recent definition. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://population.un.org/wup/Publications/Files/WUP2018-Methodology.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the same time period is available for rural population rates. The results can be viewed by country development groups, geographic regions (i.e., Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America and the Caribbean, Northern America and Oceania), income groups, and 21 geographic subregions. Additionally, estimates and projections are available on the population of urban agglomerations with 300,000 inhabitants or more in 2018 for the period between 1950 and 2035. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/upload_worldbank_data). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

description: ### Overview Baseline water stress measures the ratio of total water withdrawals to available renewable surface and groundwater supplies. A higher ratio indicates more competition among users. These ratios were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low water stress (<10%) to extremely high water stress (>80%). Water withdrawals include domestic, industrial, irrigation and livestock consumptive and non-consumptive uses. Available renewable water supplies include surface and groundwater supplies and the impact of upstream consumptive water use and large dams on downstream water availability. Water stress values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6). ### Methodology Aqueduct used the global hydrological model, PCRaster Global Water Balance (PCR-GLOBWB 2), to calculate five indicators. Baseline water stress is one of those indicators and was calculated using the gross and net total withdrawal and available water per sub-basin time series from the default model run. The model was first used to calculate a time series of water stress per catchment per month. To calculate water stress, total withdrawals were divided by the available renewable surface and groundwater supplies. Net consumptive water use was subtracted from the total available renewable water supply before the ratio was calculated. The results were output in 12 monthly time series time series of water stress per sub-basin. Water resources in delta sub-basins were pooled. Next, the time series were converted into baseline values using an ordinary least squares (OLS) regression. For example, the regression output for January 2020 represents the chronic, long-term condition of water stress in January’s from 1960 to 2020. This was repeated for every month and then averaged into an annual value. All raw values were limited to a maximum of 100% and a minimum of 0%. Sub-basins that were classified “Arid and low water use” were handled separately and were given a raw value for baseline water stress of -1. Finally, raw baseline water stress values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw baseline water stress values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds. - Low (0-1): < 10% - Low to medium (1-2): 10-20% - Medium to high (2-3): 20-40% - High (3-4): 40-80% - Extremely high (4-5): >80% - Arid and low water use (5): -1 For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

For example, the average minimum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the minimum temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average minimum temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in annual average minimum temperature is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual average minimum temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting and averaging all daily minimum temperature data over a given year. The average annual minimum temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average minimum temperature. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average minimum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual minimum temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The cumulative precipitation for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by adding all daily precipitation data over a given year. The cumulative precipitations were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in cumulative precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that cumulative precipitation is decreasing. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the cumulative precipitation in 2000 was calculated as an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows projected change NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4ca6826c-718d-457d-b4e2-e9277d7ed62c), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3d8e2e82-b33a-4898-90e5-6e4a1d007b82), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c4b12251-2d61-458f-a2c0-096c37901ade), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/1d2f4eae-10e1-4ea6-980c-501b34106de2), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d3f512c0-fbb0-47d5-9ac9-a452574c8e58), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3941bbba-181b-434a-84c3-fcdfa5234735), [Projected Change in Dry Spells](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d0f46576-411d-48aa-8df8-d89a3792cdce), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/66d28bbc-1e6e-4156-9ba2-875ecab665af). description: The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset shows the change in annual average temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Average Annual Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual average temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis using the following steps: All daily low temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average low temperature value. All daily high temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average high temperature value. Average annual temperature was calculated by taking the mean of the average daily temperature over a given year. Average daily temperature was calculated by dividing the sum of daily low temperature and daily high temperature by 2. The average annual temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average temperature. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual average temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

description: The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average days of extreme precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme precipitation day is defined as a day where precipitation is greater than the 99th percentile precipitation compared to the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Days of extreme precipitation are divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation dataset provides projections on how extreme precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Generally, extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation dataset was created with precipitation data from LOCA. The LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual average extreme precipitation days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily precipitation values for a given year and summing the number of days where precipitation was greater than the 99th percentile precipitation during the baseline period. The annual average extreme precipitation days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in extreme precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

description: The non-CO₂ agricultural emissions data set, published the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in its FAOSTAT database, contains all the non-CO₂ emissions produced in the different agricultural emissions subdomains (enteric fermentation, manure management, rice cultivation, synthetic fertilizers, manure applied to soils, manure left on pastures, crop residues, cultivation of organic soils, burning of crop residues, burning of savanna, energy use) and provides a picture of their contribution to the total amount of GHG emissions from agriculture. GHG emissions from agriculture tabulated here consist of non-CO₂ gases—namely, methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O)—produced by crop and livestock production and management activities. The FAOSTAT emissions database is computed following Tier 1 IPCC 2006 Guidelines for National GHG Inventories. GHG emissions data are provided by countries, regions, and special groups, with global coverage, relative to the period 1961-present (with annual updates) and with projections for 2030 and 2050. GHG emissions are expressed as Gg CO₂ and CO₂e (from CH₄ and N₂O), by underlying agricultural emission subdomain and by aggregate (agriculture total, agriculture total plus energy, agricultural soils). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

As nations urbanize and citizens become wealthier, people generally increase the share of resource-intensive foods—such as meats and dairy—in their diets. Ruminant meats (beef, lamb, goat), are particularly resource-intensive. Although some of this shift reflects health and welfare gains for many people, shifts to high-meat diets will make it harder for the world to achieve several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, including those on hunger, healthy lives, water management, climate change, and terrestrial ecosystems. The availability of ruminant meat data represent retail-level availability of ruminant meats (beef, lamb, goat) per capita per day across the world, from 1961-2013, with a "business as usual" projection, RCP 8.5, out to 2050. Data for 1961-2013 are from FAO's Food Balance Sheets. Data for 2050 are from FAO's projection of food demand and production. Because FAO projects that sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia in 2050 will still have insufficient calories to feed everyone adequately, WRI adjusted food amounts upward in those two regions to ensure 3,000 calories are available per person per day in all regions. Data for 2014-2050 are linear interpolations between observed (2013) and projected (2050) data. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The consumption Footprint in global hectares (ha) includes the area needed to produce the materials consumed and the area needed to absorb the carbon dioxide emissions. The consumption footprint of a nation is calculated in the National Footprint Accounts as a nation’s primary production footprint plus the footprint of imports minus the footprint of exports, and is thus, strictly speaking, a footprint of apparent consumption. The national average of per capita consumption footprint is equal to a country’s consumption footprint divided by its population. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. The Agriculture Production Value data set is published by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in its FAOSTAT database. It includes national data on gross and net production values, in current US$, and gross production values in constant and current US$ and local currency units, for various food and agriculture commodities and aggregates thereof, expressed in both total value and value per capita, spanning 1961-2014. Value of gross production is compiled by multiplying gross production in physical terms by output prices at farm gate. Value of gross production measures production in monetary terms at the farm gate level. Since intermediate uses within the agricultural sector (seed and feed) have not been subtracted from production data, this value of production aggregate refers to the notion of "gross production.” Value of gross production is provided in both current and constant terms and is expressed in U.S. dollars and standard local currency (SLC). The current value of production measures value in the prices relating to the period being measured. It thus represents the market value of food and agricultural products at the time they were produced. Value of production in constant terms is derived using the average prices of a selected year or years, known as the base period. Constant price series can be used to show how the quantity or volume of products has changed, and are often referred to as volume measures. The ratio of the current and constant price series gives a measure of price movements. U.S. dollar figures for value of gross production are converted from local currencies using official exchange rates as prevailing in the respective years. The SLC of a country is the local currency prevailing in the latest year. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. ### Overview The Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 4 (GAEZ v4) dataset assesses current and future agricultural resources and their potential. It is a standardized framework allowing for the characterization of climate, soil, and terrain conditions that are relevant for agricultural production. Data from the Fourth theme, Suitability and Attainable Yield, is displayed here. It combines multiple inputs ranging from climatic conditions, water supply, and agricultural input levels to spatially map the suitability of 4 different crops globally. Outputs are presented at 5 arc minutes resolution, which is approximately 9 km x 9 km at the equator but [changes with distance from the equator](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616). ​​Information on the current and future use of land resources are important for agricultural decision-making with implications on food security, sustainability of land and water resources, and agricultural development and policies. The GAEZ v4 dataset brings together multiple data sources to provide information on current crop suitability and assess its potential impact from climate change. Coffee, Cotton, Dryland Rice, and Wetland Rice are important commodities around the globe and the Crop Suitability Class provides important spatial information on where these commodities will thrive or face challenges in future timeframes and under different climate scenarios. Understanding what changes may occur in the future will enable different actors the ability to increase resilience, develop techniques or policies to alleviate potential challenges, and maintain food security. The Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations (FAO) together with the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) began developing the GAEZ modeling framework in the early 1980s to provide current data on the state of agricultural resources. It has since expanded to support sustainable agricultural development and provide key information on current and future risks to agricultural production, crop development, land productivity, and impacts from climate change. ### Methodology Multiple datasets were used as inputs to the GAEZ v4 modeling framework and provide data on historic and future climate attributes, soil and terrain resources, land cover, protected land, biodiversity areas, water resources, administrative units, population, and livestock. Historical climate data comes from the Climatic Research Unit TS v3.21 datasets which include monthly climate information. Future climate data is derived from multiple climate model outputs for four (2.6, 4.5, 6, 8.5) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) from the Fifth Assessment Report (AR5) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Data processing was broken into several steps and seven main modules summarize the necessary steps within the GAEZ v4 modeling framework. Outputs from each of the modules are categorized into six main themes: 1) Land and Water Resources, 2) Agro-climatic Resources, 3) Agro-climatic Potential Yield, 4) Suitability and Attainable Yield, 5) Actual Yields and Production, and 6) Yield and Production Gaps. The Suitability Class sub-theme falls under Theme Four of the outputs and Module V of the modeling framework. Module V integrates results from the first four modules and combines agro-climatic potential yields with soil and terrain evaluation results. This Module identifies in each grid cell its respective soil types and slope classes and then assesses and assigns a suitability rating and simulated potential yield. Results are then aggregated and mapped for each historic and future 30-year period by crop, input level, and water source and have a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes (approximately 9 km at the equator). Suitability classes are calculated from the normalized Suitability Index (SI), where: SI = 100 x (90 x VS + 70 x S + 50 x MS + 30 x mS + 15 x VmS + 0 x NS) / 0.9 SI values can range from 0 to 10,000 and the acronyms that are underlying suitability classes are defined as follows: VS = very suitable, S = suitable, MS = moderately suitable, mS = marginally suitable, VmS = very marginally suitable, and NS = not suitable. These six categories represent the shares of area extents of the different suitability classes in a grid cell. SI is calculated for each of the 53 crops by the level of input, management, and water supply system. The resultant SI in each grid cell is then grouped into eight classes depicting the aggregate crop suitability as: - Very high: SI > 8,500 - High: 7,000 < SI ≤ 8,500 - Good: 5,550 < SI ≤ 7,000 - Medium: 4,000 < SI ≤ 5,500 - Moderate: 2,500 < SI ≤ 4,000 - Marginal: 1,000 < SI ≤ 2,500 - Very marginal: 0 < SI ≤ 1,000 - Not suitable: SI = 0 For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.fao.org/3/cb4744en/cb4744en.pdf). ### Additional Information Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. The Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 4 Crop Suitability Index full dataset has data for 53 crops, additional timeframes (1961-1990, 1971-2000, and 2071-2100), RCPs (2.6 and 6.0), water supply (rainfed all phases, gravity irrigation), a low input level option, and a without CO2 fertilization option. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. See the documentation on how we retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/blob/master/foo_067_rw0_crop_suitability_class). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

### Overview The Food from the Sea dataset on Resource Watch presents a record of the production, import, export, caloric supply, and protein supply from ocean-sourced food (also known as ‘blue food’) in a country’s food supply from 1961 to 2018. This indicator takes into account marine plants and animals as well as their processed food derivatives and is measured in kilocalories per person per day. This data comes from the Food Balance Sheets produced by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), and is aggregated by the Resource Watch team to sum all ocean-derived food commodities. Fish and plant production from the sea has increased over time, providing an important food source for many across the globe. Although fish provided an average of only about 35 calories per capita per day in 2017, according to the [FAO](http://www.fao.org/3/ca9229en/ca9229en.pdf), fish play an important role in global food provision, accounting for about 17 percent of animal protein and 7 percent of all protein consumed by humans. This number is even higher in some developing regions and many small island developing states, which derive 50 percent or more of their animal protein from aquatic foods. The ocean contributes a major portion of the world’s fish products, with ocean-based production representing nearly 90 percent of global landings from capture fisheries and about a third of aquaculture production. As the global population and people’s incomes rise, the demand for ocean-derived food will continue to grow. [By some estimates](http://www.fao.org/fileadmin/templates/wsfs/docs/expert_paper/How_to_Feed_the_World_in_2050.pdf), nearly 500 million metric tons of animal meat will be required to feed the global population in 2050. Because of its reduced impact on climate change, feed efficiency, production potential, nutrition, and accessibility, food from the sea [has a large potential to meet this need](https://oceanpanel.org/sites/default/files/2019-11/19_HLP_BP1%20Paper.pdf). The FAO Food Balance Sheets (FBS) present a comprehensive and consolidated resource for assessing the pattern of a country’s food supply and its utilization on an annual basis. The FBS data are generally used to support policy analysis and decision-making, to provide an assessment of self-sufficiency, to estimate whether nutritional requirements are met, and as a major element for projection of food demand. For fish and fish products, they also represent a useful tool to monitor the development in overall domestic fish availability and utilization, reveal changes in the types of species consumed, and give an indication of the role of fish in total food supply and its share in animal and overall proteins. ### Methodology Food Balance Sheets (FBS) are compiled every year by FAO, mainly with country-level data on the production and trade of food commodities. Using this data and the available information on loss coefficients, stock changes, and types of utilization, available food supplies are calculated. This is achieved by taking domestic production (capture fisheries and aquaculture), minus non-food uses, minus exports, plus imports, plus or minus variation in stocks. Specific food composition factors are then applied to the related supply of each product type in order to obtain calories, proteins and fats. In order to have comparable statistics applicable to all countries in the world, data are then converted into primary equivalent (live weight equivalent, i.e. the weight of the fish at the time of harvest) using specific technical conversion factors. The per capita supply of each item available for human consumption is then obtained by dividing the respective quantity by the resident population. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://fenixservices.fao.org/faostat/static/documents/FBS/New%20FBS%20methodology.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for other commodities and food supply components as well as the full time series are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. The FAO Food Balance Sheet data was aggregated by the Resource Watch team by summing the total dietary energy supply coming from ocean-derived food commodities by country. The FAO Food Balance Sheet categories that were considered ocean-derived food commodities and summed include: Demersal Fish (2762); Pelagic Fish (2763); Marine Fish, Other (2764); Crustaceans (2765); Cephalopods (2766); Molluscs, Other (2767); Meat, Aquatic Mammals (2768); Aquatic Animals, Others (2769); Aquatic Plants (2775); Fish, Body Oil (2781); and Fish, Liver Oil (2782). See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/foo_061_rw0_blue_food_supply). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata and the [The Future of Food from the Sea Blue Paper](https://oceanpanel.org/sites/default/files/2019-11/19_HLP_BP1%20Paper.pdf) commissioned by the High Level Panel for a Sustainable Ocean Economy.

description: The German Federal Institute for Geosciences and Natural Resources (BGR) partnered with UNESCO's International Hydrological Programme and the International Association of Hydrogeologists to coordinate the World-wide Hydrogeological Mapping and Assessment Programme (WHYMAP). WHYMAP’s goal is to collect, combine and visualize global hydrogeological data to raise awareness of groundwater resources and promote global discussion on water issues. The Groundwater Environments and Recharge Rates Map is a global map of groundwater resources at a scale of 1:25,000,000 and is used to characterize major groundwater environments and recharge rates. The maps used to characterize groundwater environments were selected by evaluating national, regional and continental maps at scales of 1:1,000,000 to 1:15,000,000. Maps at each of these scales were examined to develop continental maps at a scale of 1:10,000,000, which could then be combined into a global map. Differences in each map’s level of detail, philosophy, approach, hydrogeological interpretation and projection had to be considered when combining these maps. These maps were reviewed and redrawn to improve the consistency of methods for each continent. Hydrogeological mapping experts from different parts of the world contributed their regional knowledge to the final revision of these continental maps before they were combined into a final global map. Groundwater recharge rates represent the years 1961-1990. These values are derived from simulations with the global hydrological model WaterGAP, version 2.1f from the University of Frankfurt/Main, Germany. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. ### Overview The ReefBase Coral Bleaching and Coral Diseases dataset provides observation details of coral bleaching and disease occurrences around the world. The data indicates observations of global coral reefs, whether there was observed disease or bleaching, and if so, the type of disease or severity of the bleaching. The data was compiled by the United Nations Environment Programme’s World Conservation Monitoring Center (UNEP-WCMC) and have been updated by ReefBase since 2002. ### Methodology Coral disease and bleaching data is sourced from literature, postings on the [coral-list](http://www.coral.noaa.gov/lists/), the ReefBase online [Bleaching Report](http://www.reefbase.org/contribute/bleachingreport.aspx), and through collaborations with numerous institutions and individuals. The National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS), and Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority (GBRMPA) also contributed to the dataset. ### Overview The Population Below Income Poverty Line ($3.20) dataset shows the percentage of the population living below a $3.20 a day poverty line in 2011 international prices. The $3.20 poverty line is derived from typical national poverty lines in countries classified as Lower Middle Income. The dataset is created by comparing the $3.20 poverty line to income and consumption data from each country. Income and consumption data allows researchers to determine the cost of living and the cost of goods and services in each country based on 2011 pricing. This is used to convert the $3.20 poverty line into local currencies and poverty rates. The dataset is published for low- and middle-income countries, countries eligible to receive World Bank loans, and recently graduated countries only. It is available for all years from 1967-present and has a national spatial resolution. The dataset was created by the World Bank as part of its internationally comparable poverty monitoring database. The database serves to monitor poverty rates for all countries and utilizes different poverty rates for different country income classifications. The World Bank Group is committed to reducing extreme poverty to 3 percent or less, globally, by 2030. Monitoring poverty is important on the global development agenda as well as on the national development agenda of many countries. ### Methodology The Population below Income Poverty Line ($3.20) dataset was created as part of the World Bank’s Poverty Measures of the Developing World database to calculate the poverty headcount ratio per country at a $3.20 a day poverty line. The poverty headcount ratio is the proportion of a population that lives below the poverty line. First, researchers determined the international poverty line to create a common standard of what “poverty” is. This was first done in the 1980’s by looking at academic papers on the economies of 22 developing countries and a poverty line of $1 a day was created. Since then new and updated international poverty lines have been created and as of 2015 the World Bank has used an international poverty line of $1.90 a day at 2011 purchasing power parity (PPP). This was created by averaging the national poverty lines of 15 of the poorest countries ranked by per capita consumption. The dataset shown here uses a more liberal poverty line of $3.20, which is based on low- and middle- income countries. It is based on 2011 PPP, which means the monetary value is representative of the cost of specific goods in each country as of 2011 and highlights the differences in absolute purchasing power between economies. International poverty lines cannot be directly compared with poverty measured at national poverty lines in local currency, which reflect economy-specific decisions of poverty. To make them comparable and determine the rate of poverty in a country the international poverty line was applied to each country individually. To do this, income and consumption data from household surveys across 164 countries in six regions and 25 other high income countries were used to determine household living standards. The poverty line at 2011 PPP was converted into local currencies in 2011 prices and then converted to the prices of goods at the time of the relevant nationally representative household survey using the best available Consumer Price Index (CPI). CPI is a measure of the cost of consumer goods and services at a given time. Then the poverty rate was calculated by determining how much of the country's population fell below the $3.20 2011 PPP poverty line. The population living below the poverty line was then divided by the country’s total population and multiplied by 100 to create the final dataset. Nationally representative household surveys were conducted by national statistical offices or by private agencies under the supervision of government or international agencies and obtained from government statistical offices and World Bank Group operational departments. CPI data was primarily taken from the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF’s) International Financial Statistics. To make national poverty rates comparable between countries they were calculated and shown for individual years, known as reference years. This required interpolating and extrapolating data for countries that lacked survey data for each year. This was done by adjusting the mean income or expenditure observed in a survey year by a country’s growth factor to estimate the unknown survey data in the reference year. For the full documentation, please see this [methodology document](http://iresearch.worldbank.org/PovcalNet/methodology.aspx) or click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. ### Overview The Gini index measures economic inequality in a country. Specifically, it is the extent to which the distribution of income (or, in some cases, consumption expenditure) deviates from a perfectly equal distribution among individuals or households within an economy. A Gini index of 0 represents perfect equality, while an index of 100 implies perfect inequality. The Gini index dataset was released by the World Bank. This data is reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is updated annually and is available for the years 1967-present, though most countries only have data for a subset of these years. ### Methodology The Gini Index was calculated from the World Bank’s internationally comparable poverty monitoring database, which draws on income or detailed consumption data from more than 1,000 household surveys across 138 countries in 6 regions and 21 other high-income countries (industrialized economies). To calculate the Gini index, a Lorenz curve plots the cumulative percentages of total income received against the cumulative number of recipients, starting with the poorest individual or household. The Gini index measures the area between the Lorenz curve and a hypothetical (45-degree) line of absolute equality, expressed as a percentage of the maximum area under the line. For full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SI.POV.GINI/). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. ### Overview The Global Material Flows Database holds a variety of datasets on material extraction and consumption. The dataset displayed on Resource Watch shows global material consumption and extraction of nonmetallic minerals, biomass, fossil fuels, and metal ores at a national scale. This data is available at the source for every year between 1970 and 2017, but only the 2017 data is mapped on Resource Watch. The dataset also contains additional data on the overall consumption and extraction for each country at a per capita rate for the year 2015. Consumption and extraction are expressed in units of metric tons. This dataset was created using national statistics from a combination of local government organizations and international organizations like the United Nations, Eurostat, and the United States Geological Survey. This dataset was developed to assist governments in creating strategies to increase efficiency of material production and consumption activities. The dataset can help in better understanding how economic growth patterns influence resource use. It can also be used to evaluate the impacts of policies that have been adopted in the past. Additionally, the dataset can be used to develop effective strategies to minimize future resource use through targeted consumption and production policies. This database is used by academics around the world, integrated into several multi-regional input-output databases such as [EXIOBASE](https://www.exiobase.eu/) and featured in reports by international organisations, such as the United Nations Environmental Program and the European Economic Area. This database was created by the United Nations Environment Programme International Resource Panel (UNEP IRP) and developed as part of a collaborative effort by the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation, the Sustainable Resource Use research group of the Vienna University of Economics and Business, the Institute of Social Ecology Vienna, the Nagoya University, and University of Sydney’s Integrated Sustainability Analysis. ### Methodology This dataset was created by combining data from multiple sources. Data for all categories of extraction were taken from national production statistics. These datasets were collected from individual government ministries, industrial associations, and Eurostat's production statistics (PRODCOM) whenever available. Additional available data from international organizations, like the British Geological Survey and United States Geological Survey, were also used. Some categories, like metal ore extraction, were estimated using techniques in the [Eurostat: Economy-wide Material Flow Accounts Compilation Guide 2013](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/1798247/6191533/2013-EW-MFA-Guide-10Sep2013.pdf/). Data reported using different units was converted to a standard unit by using category-specific conversion factors. Data on domestic material consumption was calculated by finding the sum of each country’s domestic extraction and import values and subtracting total exports. Data on imports and exports was taken from national offices when available and United Nations reports when not available. Both per capita datasets were created by dividing each country’s total extraction and consumption by its population. The final datasets were produced in tabular format at a national level. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for categories such as crops, natural gas and petroleum are available from the data provider. For each of these categories, data on trade, raw material consumption, raw material consumption per capita, raw material inputs, raw material equivalents of imports, raw material equivalents of exports is also provided. Lastly, data for each year from 1970 to 2017 is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](72607dcf-8876-489c-94f2-28e9e10208bc) as a replacement.**_ ### Overview This dataset shows potential climate change impacts on world crop production and yield from 1970-2000 to 2080 under different emissions scenarios. The impact under different emissions scenarios is reported as the percentage change from this baseline. This dataset includes the years 2020, 2050, and 2080; the crops maize, rice, wheat, and grain; and the emissions scenarios from the Special Report on Emissions Scenarios (SRES) A1F1, A2A, A2B, A2C, B1A, B2A, and B2B. This dataset is an update to a major crop modeling study by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS). ### Methodology The initial study was published in 1997, based on output of the HadCM2 model forced with greenhouse gas (GHG) concentration from the IS95 emission scenarios in 1997. Results of the initial study are presented in “Potential Impacts of Climate Change on World Food Supply: Data Sets from a Major Crop Modeling Study,” released by the NASA Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center (SEDAC) in 2001. The co-authors developed and tested a method for investigating the spatial implications of climate change on crop production. The Decision Support System for Agrotechnology Transfer dynamic process crop growth models were specified and validated for 127 sites in the major world agricultural regions. Results from the crop models, calibrated and validated in the major crop-growing regions, were then used to test functional forms describing the response of yield changes in the climate and environmental conditions as a percent change by country. The baseline year for crop yield changes is the average yield simulated under current climate (1970-2000 baseline). The resulting yield change data was then fed into trade models to assess impacts on prices and overall food production. Optimal yield is the potential yield not limited by water or fertilizer and without management constraints. Adapted yields are evaluated in each country as a fraction of the potential yield. The weighting factor combines the ratio of current yields to current yield potential and the economic limitation of the economic country’s agricultural systems. This updated version is based on HadCM3 model output along with GHG concentrations from the Special Report on Emissions Scenarios (SRES). The crop yield estimates incorporate some major improvements: (1) consistent crop simulation methodology and climate change scenarios; (2) weighting of model site results by contribution to regional and national, and rainfed and irrigated, production; (3) quantitative foundation for estimation of physiological CO₂ effects on crop yields; (4) explicit consideration of adaptation; and (5) reporting of results by country rather than by Basic Linked System region. For full documentation, please read the source [methodology](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0959378003000827?via%3Dihub). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data is available from the data provider for the years 2020, 2050, and 2080; the crops maize, rice, wheat, and grain; and the emissions scenarios from the Special Report on Emissions Scenarios (SRES) A1F1, A2A, A2B, A2C, B1A, B2A, and B2B. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. The Climate Change Impacts on Crop Production dataset is a tabular dataset released by NASA SEDAC in collaboration with the NASA GISS. This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

### Overview This dataset details global potential evapotranspiration of a reference crop at 30 arc-seconds resolution (approximately 1km at the equator) for the 1970-2000 period. Evapotranspiration is the simultaneous process of evaporation and transpiration. Evaporation is the process in which liquid water is converted to water vapor. Transpiration is when plants take up water with their roots and release water vapor to the atmosphere through stomata in their leaves. The unit for evapotranspiration is total millimeters (mm) per year. A higher value in mm suggests more water is lost from that cropped surface. Potential evapotranspiration measures the ability of the atmosphere to remove water through evapotranspiration. In this dataset crop evapotranspiration (ET₀) is used as a measure of the evapotranspiration rate from a referenced and standardized vegetated surface (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nation ([FAO](http://www.fao.org/3/X0490E/x0490e04.htm)). This concept of ET₀ is useful to study evaporative demand of the atmosphere in relation to climatic factors and independently of crop type, crop development, and management practices. This dataset was developed by Antonio Trabucco and Robert Zomer with the support of the Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research Consortium for Spatial Information (CGIAR-CSI). The dataset can be used to support studies on sustainable development, poverty alleviation, and climate change adaptation. It is particularly relevant to crop and yield modeling and studying the impacts of climate change on future crop production. ### Methodology The widely-used standard equation to estimate potential evapotranspiration is the FAO Penman-Monteith equation (FAO-PM). Researchers used the FAO-PM equation in combination with data on multiple climate variables to produce an estimated ET₀ for a reference crop (well-watered grass at 12 cm of height). A reference crop was used to ensure the final results provided ET₀ information solely based on climate information of a region. Climate data was collected from [WorldClim 2.0 dataset](http://worldclim.org/version2). The World Clim 2.0 dataset includes monthly data on temperature, solar radiation, wind speed and water vapor pressure. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://figshare.com/articles/Global_Aridity_Index_and_Potential_Evapotranspiration_ET0_Climate_Database_v2/7504448/3). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [aridity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cli030-Land-Aridity) data from the data provider. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for monthly averaged potential evapotranspiration is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

The Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research Consortium for Spatial Information (CGIAR-CSI) supported the development of the Global-Aridity Database. This database is designed for use in models of sustainable development, biodiversity and environmental conservation, poverty alleviation, and adaption to climate change globally, in particular in developing countries, and provides data for each month between 1970 and 2000 at a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds. This data set is the aridity index (AI), which is calculated as the ratio of mean annual precipitation to mean annual potential evapotranspiration (PET), using data from the WorldClim Global Climate Database. The yearly precipitation values are available directly from the WorldClim database, and the PET values are derived from a selection of WorldClim variables. PET is a measure of the rate at which water evaporates from the Earth's surface into the atmosphere. It is influenced by several factors, including solar radiation, temperature, air humidity, and wind speed. Other contributing factors include the leaf area index of an area, as water pooling on top of leaves and tree canopies can lead to faster evaporation than if precipitating water entered the soil layer. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.
