### Overview The Maize, Rice, Soybean, and Wheat Yield Trends dataset shows the average annual change in crop yield from 1989-2008. Agricultural crop yield is the amount of crop harvested per area of land. It is used to measure a crop’s performance. This study used approximately 1.8 million agricultural census reports from 13,500 political units around the world to determine how crop yield changed over time. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes, which is approximately 10 kilometers x 10 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.” Together, maize, rice, soybean, and wheat account for nearly two-thirds of global agricultural calories. Global demand for these crops is rising as a result of diet shifts, rising population levels and increased biofuel demand. In order to meet projected demand, [crop production needs to double by 2050](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms2296#MOESM1532). Improving crop yield, instead of clearing new land for agriculture, is one of the preferred solutions. In many areas, yield is stagnant or has collapsed entirely. Understanding where improvement is most needed can guide new agricultural investments. It is also important to identify and continue improving yield of high-performing crops and regions. This dataset was produced by EarthStat, a collaboration between the Global Landscapes Initiative (GLI) at the University of Minnesota’s Institute on the Environment (UMN IonE) and the Land Use and Global Environment (LUGE) lab at the University of British Columbia (UBC). EarthStat’s mission is to provide data on the global food system to help others make science-based decisions. The GLI is a scientific initiative that develops and applies tools to characterize global land use and evaluate global agricultural supply and demand trends. The LUGE lab is a research group that studies links between land use, global environmental change, and food security. ### Methodology Approximately 1.8 million census reports were used to determine yield of the four crops for the years between 1989 and 2008. Crop yield is the ratio of production (kilograms) and harvested area (hectares). According to the UN’s [Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)](http://www.fao.org/waicent/faostat/agricult/pr_ele-e.htm), production is the amount of crop harvested. The harvested area is the area from which the crop is gathered. National-level data used in this study was provided by the [FAO](http://www.fao.org/faostat/en/#home), who collects data from the member countries’ statistical offices. At the time of the study, the FAO had crop data for 226 nations. In addition to national-level data, the study also used subnational data for the 51 countries that account for more than 70% of global production/harvested area for each of the four crops. Data was available at the state/province level for all 51 countries and county/district/município/department level for an additional 17 countries. This data was collected from these countries’ agricultural and statistical bureaus. According to the data provider, studies have used linear regression to project future crop yields. As such, the annual crop yields in this study (one data point per year) were linearly regressed to calculate the average change in yield from 1989-2008. A linear regression is a line modeled to fit the shape of a group of data points. The slope of the line gives the rate of change–in this case, the average yield change over the observed period. This calculation was performed for each crop at each political unit. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0066428#pone.0066428.s017). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The energy sector is strongly exposed to climate variability and change, from shifts in wind and solar resources to changing heating and cooling demand. Planning a resilient energy system therefore requires indicators that translate climate conditions into sector-relevant quantities. The Energy Indicators application provides wind, solar and energy-demand indicators derived from DestinE Climate Digital Twin (Climate DT) model data, enabling users to assess how energy supply and demand conditions vary in space and time and how they may change under future climate scenarios. More information can be found in the Climate DT User Guide. The application provides indicators for the energy sector: capacity factors for different wind turbines, wind speed histograms, and high- and low-wind events, alongside energy-demand indicators (heating and cooling degree-days) and a solar demand indicator (photovoltaic potential). The indicators are derived from hourly Climate DT output and provided globally at kilometre-scale resolution. By deriving these indicators consistently from Climate DT simulations, the application supports the analysis of climate-driven trends in renewable energy resources and energy demand, aiding adaptation planning across the energy sector. More information can be found in the user guide https://platform.destine.eu/docs/climate-dt-user-guide/doc/index.html

description: Precipitation is an essential variable to assess the severity of many extreme weather events. As a first assessment, it might be sufficient to look at daily rainfall totals for a given region. However, an in-depth analysis requires local information on severity, affected area and statistical return times to enable the development of fitted adaptation strategies. HydroMet fulfils this need by providing information on the intensity, duration, spatial extent and return time of extreme precipitation events over Europe based on DestinE Climate DT model data. More information can be found in the [Climate DT user guide](https://platform.destine.eu/services/documents-and-api/doc/?service_name=climate-dt-user-guide). The extreme precipitation parameters produced by HydroMet are based on existing products of the German Meteorological Service (DWD): KOSTRA2020, the latest version of KOSTRA-DWD (Shehu et al., 2023), and CatRaRE, Catalogue of Radar-based heavy Rainfall Events (Lengfeld et al., 2021). KOSTRA is a coordinated effort across German Federal states to develop methods for evaluating precipitation extremes from gauge-based observations. The system, developed over three decades, provides data about precipitation levels, duration and the annual return interval. CatRaRE is a software package able to detect and define extreme rain events and, at the same time, generate a catalogue with meteorological and geographical information for each event. At DWD, it is applied to radar data. HydroMet combines both products for a consistent dataset on the climatological scale. Shehu, B., Willems, W., Stockel, H., Thiele, L.-B., & Haberlandt, U. (2023). Regionalisation of rainfall depth–duration–frequency curves with different data types in Germany. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 27(5), 1109–1132. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-27-1109-2023 Lengfeld, K., Walawender, E., Winterrath, T., & Becker, A. (2021). CatRaRE: A Catalogue of radar-based heavy rainfall events in Germany derived from 20 years of data. Meteorologische Zeitschrift, 30(6), 469–487. https://doi.org/10.1127/metz/2021/1088

Note: This Generation 1 Collection has been superseded by Generation 2 Simulation-level Collections The DestinE Digital Twin for Climate Change Adaptation (Climate DT) supports adaptation activities by providing innovative climate information on multi-decadal timescales, globally, at scales at which many impacts of climate change are observed. It combines cutting-edge global Earth-system models, impact-sector applications and observations into a unified framework to provide global climate projections and impact-sector information on multi-decadal timescales (1990 to ~2050), at very high spatial resolutions (5 to 10 km). The Climate DT represents the first ever attempt to operationalise the production of global multi-decadal climate projections, leveraging the world-leading supercomputing facilities of the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking along with some of the leading European climate models. A concise overview of what the Climate DT aims to achieve, and of the different concepts essential for an understanding of the Digital Twin’s characteristics, is included in the [Climate DT factsheet](https://destine.ecmwf.int/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/2024.06.07_Climate-DT-Fact-Sheet_V7-2.pdf) ## Historical Simulation Starting in 1990, the forcing follows observed changes in greenhouse gases, aerosols etc. until 2020. The simulations are using standardised CMIP6 forcing. Historical simulations are essential for model evaluation and quality control as they allow a comparison to observations. ## Models The Climate DT exploits and further evolves a new generation of global storm-resolving and eddy-rich models built through a cooperative model development approach. For more information on models please click [here](https://destine.ecmwf.int/climate-change-adaptation-digital-twin-climate-dt/#models) ## Simulations The Climate DT team carries out several types of digital twin simulations on the EuroHPC supercomputers. Multi-decadal simulations are produced to cover the recent past (from 1990) and possible future evolutions of the climate up to 2050. See [here](https://destine.ecmwf.int/climate-change-adaptation-digital-twin-climate-dt/#simulations) for more information on Simulations ## Parameters Below we see the list of parameters extracted from the 'DestinE Climate DT data portfolio', for more information please refer to the page [Climate DT Phase 1 CLTE Parameters](https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/DDCZ/Climate+DT+Phase+1+data+catalogue)

description: Wildfires are strongly influenced by weather and climate conditions, particularly prolonged drought, high temperatures, low humidity and strong winds. Assessing wildfire danger therefore requires indicators that combine the effects of multiple meteorological variables into a single measure of fire-conducive conditions. The Fire Weather Index (FWI, Van Wagner 1987; Wotton 2009) application fulfils this need by providing information on wildfire danger globally based on DestinE Climate Digital Twin (Climate DT) model data. The application enables users to assess the temporal evolution, spatial distribution and long-term changes of fire weather conditions and associated wildfire risk. More information can be found in the [User Guide](https://platform.destine.eu/docs/climate-dt-user-guide/doc/index.html). The FWI application is based on the Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System, one of the most widely used operational wildfire danger rating systems worldwide. The system combines temperature, relative humidity, wind speed and precipitation to estimate the moisture content of different fuel layers and the potential behaviour of wildfires. The output includes the Fire Weather Index (FWI), which is calculated using the Fine Fuel Moisture Code (FFMC), Duff Moisture Code (DMC), Drought Code (DC), Initial Spread Index (ISI), and Buildup Index (BUI). Together, these components describe the likelihood of ignition, fuel availability, and potential fire intensity. By applying the Fire Weather Index System consistently to Climate DT simulations, the application provides a harmonized assessment of current and future fire weather conditions, enabling the analysis of extreme fire seasons, climate-driven trends in wildfire danger and regional differences in fire-prone environments across Europe. Van Wagner, C. E. (1987). Development and structure of the Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System. Forestry Technical Report 35, Canadian Forestry Service. Wotton, B. M. (2009). Interpreting and using outputs from the Canadian Forest Fire Danger Rating System in research applications. Environmental and Ecological Statistics, 16, 107-131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10651-007-0084-2

description: Land surface hydrology governs the availability of water for ecosystems, agriculture and human use, and its response to climate change is a key concern for adaptation planning. The HydroLand application provides land surface hydrology indicators, including soil moisture, discharge and aridity, derived from DestinE Climate Digital Twin (Climate DT) model data. The application enables users to assess the spatial distribution, seasonal variability and long-term changes of hydrological conditions. More information can be found in the Climate DT User Guide. HydroLand is based on the Mesoscale Hydrologic Model (mHM, mhm-ufz.org), a distributed hydrological model that simulates the terrestrial water cycle from meteorological forcing. mHM is driven by Climate DT output to produce fluxes such as river discharge, evapotranspiration and soil moisture, which are then processed into user-oriented indicators covering soil moisture, discharge, and aridity. The dataset also includes the original mHM outputs and figures documenting model validation and selected results. By applying mHM consistently to Climate DT simulations, the application provides a harmonised assessment of current and future hydrological conditions globally, supporting the analysis of drought, water availability and climate-driven trends in the terrestrial water cycle.

description: ### Overview The Gross Domestic Product Per Capita dataset shows gross domestic product (GDP) per person based on purchasing power parity (PPP), converted to international dollars. GDP is the sum of the value of all the goods and services produced within a nation in a given year. PPP equalizes each country’s purchasing power by controlling for differences in price levels between economies. An international dollar has the same purchasing power over GDP as the U.S. dollar has in the United States. In other words, an international dollar would buy a comparable amount of goods and services in any country that a U.S. dollar would buy in the United States. Data is shown for each year between 1990 and present at a national resolution. The World Bank Group International Comparison Program (World Bank Group ICP) estimates PPPs for the world’s economies in order to provide comparable price and volume measures of GDP. This dataset lets users compare national GDP between countries, currencies, and time. PPPs and underlying World Bank Group ICP data are utilized for a wide variety of analyses at the global, regional, and national levels and cover many themes under the economic, environmental, and social development umbrellas. They can be used not only by the development community and researchers, but by policymakers, the media, and the wider public. The World Bank Group ICP is one of the largest statistical initiatives in the world. It relies on a partnership of international, regional, sub-regional, and national agencies working under a robust governance framework and following an established statistical methodology. Its main objectives are to produce PPPs for participating countries and to convert GDP and its expenditure components into a common currency. ### Methodology The Gross Domestic Product Per Capita dataset has three major components for its methodology: - The System of National Accounts (SNA) definition of final expenditures on GDP - The basket of goods and services from which items are selected for pricing - The methodology used to compute PPPs, within and across regions The SNA uses national expenditures as weights to aggregate PPPs through the various levels of aggregation up to GDP. The basket of goods and services, also known as the global core list of items, is used to compare the same items between different countries within a region. The methodology used to compute PPPs is based on two approaches: the Jevons index by Gini-Éltető-Köves-Szulc (GEKS) and the country product dummy method. More in-depth information about these methods can be found in the World Bank Group ICP’s document on [Measuring the Real Size of the World Economy](http://pubdocs.worldbank.org/en/927971487091799574/ICPBook-eBook-FINAL.pdf). Each participating economy also provides the following required data: - National annual average prices for a selection of items chosen from a common basket - A breakdown of national expenditures in local currency according to a common classification - Market exchange rates - Population The national average prices and national expenditures are used to calculate PPPs and are reported by participating economies in their local currencies. Both cover the whole range of final goods and services constituting the GDP. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.worldbank.org/en/programs/icp#6). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows data from the World Bank Group ICP for [Gross Domestic Product (PPP, Current International $)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Gross-Domestic-Product). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The data provider has additional data on gross domestic product separated into 44 expenditure headings, national accounts expenditures in PPP, and price level indices available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/upload_worldbank_data). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

We recommend using [this dataset](23f41bb2-2312-41ab-aaf2-ef584f80b31a) as a replacement.**_ The Municipal Waste Generated per Capita data represent trends in amounts of municipal waste (including household) produced, and the treatment and disposal method used. The amount of waste generated in each country is related to the rate of urbanization, the types and pattern of consumption, household revenue, and lifestyles. Data are provided by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) member countries' authorities through the questionnaire on the state of the environment (OECD/Eurostat) from 1990 through 2015. They were updated or revised on the basis of data from other national and international sources available to the OECD Secretariat, and on the basis of comments received from national delegates. Selected updates were also done in the context of the OECD Environmental Performance Reviews. The data are harmonized through the work of the OECD Working Party on Environmental Information (WPEI) and benefit from continued data quality efforts in OECD member countries, the OECD itself, and other international organizations. ### Overview This dataset includes the percentage of the population with access to electricity from 1990 to present, at the country level. The data represents electricity access in the urban population of each country. Access to electricity is crucial to improving the standard of living and is one of the most obvious indications of a country’s energy poverty status. Securing electricity services while decarbonizing power systems is a key challenge for developing countries, as electricity generation from fossil fuels contributes to climate change. While this dataset shows access to electricity at the national level, Resource Watch also shows data for the percentage of [rural](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene012b-Access-to-Electricity-Rural) and [national](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene012a-Access-to-Electricity) population with access to electricity. This dataset comes from a Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) database from the SE4ALL Global Tracking Framework led jointly by the World Bank, the International Energy Agency (IEA), and the Energy Sector Management Assistance Program (ESMAP). ### Methodology Electrification data is collected from industry, national surveys, and international sources. Data generally comes from nationally representative household surveys like national censuses. ### Overview This dataset shows energy intensity in 259 countries from 1990 to 2015. Energy intensity indicates how much primary energy (energy that comes directly from nature and has not been converted to a different form) is used to produce one unit of gross domestic product (GDP). GDP is a key economic indicator that measures the monetary value of goods and services provided within an area. Energy intensity is expressed as megajoules (MJ) of primary energy available per GDP produced, based on [purchasing power parity (PPP)](https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/basics/ppp.htm) in 2011 U.S. dollars (USD). PPP is a factor used to convert local currencies to one comparable unit of measure based on the local cost of goods and services in each country. Low energy intensity is desirable, as it means that less energy is used to produce one more unit of economic output. Having a low energy intensity indicates that a country can increase its economic growth without having to rely as heavily on energy consumption. The dataset was published as part of the Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) initiative. The database is intended to help policymakers in government, business, and civil society work toward doubling the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix by 2030. Resource Watch also shows [renewable energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene021a-Renewable-Energy-Consumption) and [percentage of energy consumption from renewable sources](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bced4001-425a-4fad-8c22-8214d9340ea4) data from the SE4ALL Database. ### Methodology Energy intensity was measured as the ratio of total primary energy supply to the value added to the economy. Primary energy supply data came from the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the United Nations (UN) Energy Statistics Database. The value added to the economy was expressed in 2011 USD, adjusted for PPP. The data for GDP PPP came from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://trackingsdg7.esmap.org/methodology). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [renewable energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/431f7c9e-7ef5-4f00-a5dc-8845fcb3a9a9) and [percentage of energy consumption from renewable sources](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bced4001-425a-4fad-8c22-8214d9340ea4) data from the SE4ALL Database. ### Overview The Agricultural Trade data and statistics compiled by the Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations (FAO) are key economic indicators, used to track trade flows between nations. Metrics are aggregated annually at the country level. The dataset comprises four categories: import quantity, import value, export quantity, and export value, and are available for all food and agricultural products for each country in the world. Quantity data is measured in weight (tonnes), while value is measured in 1,000 United States Dollars (USD). Agricultural commodity flows are especially important for actors along the agricultural supply chain. The metrics included in this dataset are standardized across countries, enabling comparisons to be made. This provides important information about what commodities are in surplus/deficit at the national level and elucidate linkages in the global flow of agricultural goods. The FAO has an institutional mandate to “collect, analyze, interpret, and disseminate information relating to nutrition, food and agriculture.” A primary purpose of this dataset is to ensure that there is a source of current, relevant, and reliable statistics for crop and livestock products that is applicable on the global scale. ### Methodology The FAO collects trade data from various entities including the United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD), Eurostat, and other national authorities. Trade data is collected, processed, and disseminated according to the standards outlined by the International Merchandise Trade Statistics (IMTS) [Methodology](https://unstats.un.org/unsd/trade/default.asp). The database includes annual information on the import quantity, export quantity, import value, and export value of all crop and livestock products for all countries in the world. Our data catalog only shows certain products that are derived from three crops: coffee, cotton, and rice. Additionally, only data from 1990 to 2020 is shown here , as it provides a firm historical understanding of these metrics. Trade quantity refers to the net weight (in tonnes) of the commodity and excludes containers. Export quantities are defined by IMTS methodology as the physical quantity of crop products originating or manufactured in and shipped out of the reporting country and include [re-exports](https://unstats.un.org/wiki/display/comtrade/Re-exports+and+Re-imports). Import quantity is essentially the reverse: referring to the import of products for domestic consumption or processing within that country and includes re-imports. Trade values (measured in one thousand USD) are reported as the value of the products or goods as well as the value of the services performed to deliver the goods from border to border. Trade data is compiled by the domestic customs office. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://unstats.un.org/wiki/display/comtrade/Re-exports+and+Re-imports). ### Additional Information Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for every year between 1961 and 2020 and more crops and livestock products are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data See the documentation on how our team retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/com_039_rw0_agricultural_trade_statistics). ### Overview The Urban Population Living in Slums is a global dataset that shows the percentage of a country's urban population living in slum households. A slum household is defined as a group of individuals living under the same roof lacking one or more of the following facilities: improved water, improved sanitation, sufficient living area, durable housing, and security of tenure. The dataset includes information on 97 countries utilizing the most recent survey and census data available, which ranges between 1990 and present, depending on the country. The dataset is presented at a national resolution. This dataset was created as part of the United Nations Millennium Development Goals (MDG) and was compiled by The United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN-HABITAT). The overall goal of MDG is to fight poverty in its many dimensions. This dataset was created to be used as an indicator for MDG Target 7D. Target 7D’s goal is by 2020, to have achieved a significant improvement in the lives of at least 100 million slum dwellers. ### Methodology The Urban Population Living in Slums dataset was created by using a proxy measurement based on access to some basic facilities. A household was determined to be living in a slum if atleast one of the following services were unavailable to them: - Access to improved drinking water sources that are protected from outside contamination and in particular from contamination with fecal matter. - Access to improved sanitation services that hygienically separates human waste from human contact. - Durable house that can protect its residents from extremes of climatic conditions, such as rain, heat, cold and humidity. - Sufficient living area so that more than three people don't have to share the same room that is a minimum of four square meters in area. - Secure tenure which ensures all individuals and groups have effective protection by the State against forced unlawful evictions. This data was collected by combining information from a variety of household surveys. Household surveys used varied by region and country, but included Urban Inequities Surveys (UIS), Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS), Demographic Health Surveys (DHS), World Health Surveys (WHS), Living Standards and Measurement Surveys (LSMS), Core Welfare Indicator Questionnaires (CWIQ), and the Pan Arab Project for Family Health Surveys (PAPFAM). The number of people living in urban households that were determined to be lacking one or more basic service was divided by the total urban population, and then multiplied by 100 to create the final value. National Statistics Offices typically carried out household surveys every 3-5 years and population censuses every 10 years. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://mdgs.un.org/unsd/mi/wiki/7-10-Proportion-of-urban-population-living-in-slums.ashx). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The Access to Improved Sanitation Facilities data set, derived by the Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) of the World Health Organization (WHO) and United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), is the percentage of the national population (rural, urban, and total) using improved sanitation facilities for more than 200 countries from 1990 to present. Improved sanitation facilities are likely to ensure hygienic separation of human excreta from human contact, and range from simple but protected pit latrines to flush toilets with a sewerage connection. To be effective, facilities must be correctly constructed and properly maintained. The data set is created based on national censuses and nationally representative household surveys. The coverage rates for sanitation are based on information from service users on the facilities their households actually use rather than on information from service providers, which may include nonfunctioning systems. The Climate Analysis Indicators Tool (CAIT) Emissions Projections is part of the larger CAIT Climate Data Explorer. CAIT is a suite of online data and visualization tools that support the many dimensions of climate policy making. It provides free, open, user-friendly access to world-class climate data. The projections tool allows users to view projected emissions from national and international sources and compare policy assumptions and drivers between countries and among sources. The tool aims to increase the transparency of each scenario by publishing key assumptions and other related information. The CAIT Emissions Projections tool collates emission projections for major emitters through the year 2100, or earlier if limited data are available. Each data subset, such as GHG Emissions Data or Socioeconomic Data, has indicators, such as Gross Domestic Product or Population, that influence the projection. Predictions are created through scenarios. These describe possible future pathways under existing policies and actions, or, in other words, in the absence of further mitigation efforts. CAIT draws on key climate-relevant data from respected research centers, government agencies, and international bodies. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. ### Overview This dataset shows renewable energy consumption in 259 countries from 1990 to present. In this dataset, renewable energy sources are defined as hydropower, solid and liquid biofuels, wind, solar, biogas, geothermal, marine, and waste to energy. The dataset was published as part of the Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) initiative, and the data was compiled by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the United Nations Statistics Divisions (UNSD). IEA and UNDC are the primary developers of internationally comparable national energy statistics. This dataset tracks the progress of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator 7.2, to advance the target of increase substantially the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix by 2030. Resource Watch also shows [energy intensity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene029a-Energy-Intensity) and [percentage of energy consumption from renewable sources](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bced4001-425a-4fad-8c22-8214d9340ea4) data from the SE4ALL Database. ### Methodology This dataset was compiled using data from the International Energy Agency (IEA) energy statistics, complemented by the United Nations (UN) database when IEA data was not available. IEA data contained the most comprehensive and accurate data for countries that were a part of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), as well as 75 non-OECD countries. In the case of smaller non-OECD countries, extrapolations of country data provided by the UN Statistics Division were used. ### Overview The EDGAR-FOOD dataset provides greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from food production at the global level over the time period 1990 to 2015. It was created from the [Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research (EDGARv5.0)](https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/), which is a global database of anthropogenic emissions of greenhouse gases and air pollution. EDGAR-FOOD tracks GHG emissions including carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons (PFCs), sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆), and nitrous oxide (N₂O). The emissions visualized in Resource Watch are reported in metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (Mt CO₂e) and comprise the following stages of the food production chain: - land use and land-use change - primary production of food commodities - food processing - food distribution including packaging, transport, and retail - food consumption including domestic activities of food preparation - end of life of food including food residues management and management of non-food residues used in previous food-system stages EDGAR-FOOD provides a picture of how an evolving world food system has responded to the evolution of world population in the last 25 years, together with changes in dietary habits and food related technology. At the global level, decoupling between population growth and food-related emissions is visible with emissions growing at a lower rate compared to population growth. Unlike overall GHGs emissions, the food production sector is not overwhelmingly dominated by CO₂ emissions from fossil fuels; land-based emissions are particularly relevant. Nevertheless, in line with the ongoing socio-economic development trends, food emissions are being increasingly determined by energy use, industrial activities and waste management. From the mitigation point of view, such a trend suggests that the food sector will need specific sectoral energy efficiency and decarbonisation policies. Moreover, EDGAR-FOOD is crucial to the anticipation of future changes in the overall food system in order to design efficient mitigation strategies that avoid creating additional emissions in non-targeted sectors. This dataset was generated by the European Commission Joint Research Center (EC JRC) as part of their efforts for effectively monitoring the global food system GHG emissions, in line with the strategies to work on an integrated view of the food system, such as the new [European Commission’s Farm to Fork strategy](https://ec.europa.eu/food/horizontal-topics/farm-fork-strategy_en). ### Methodology The quantification of food-system GHG emissions is done using the EDGARv5.0 as the underlying source of global GHG and air pollutants at country scale. Emissions are calculated using a bottom-up methodology complying with IPCC guidelines, with high sectoral disaggregation. GHG emissions are computed in EDGARv5.0 mostly following the [IPCC Tier 1 approach](https://www.reddcompass.org/mgd-content-v1/dita-webhelp/en/Box1.html), while a [Tier 2](https://www.reddcompass.org/mgd-content-v1/dita-webhelp/en/Box1.html) method is applied to estimate emissions from cattle enteric fermentation, rice cultivation, waste treatment and cement production. [Food and Agriculture Organization Corporate Statistical Database (FAOSTAT)] (http://www.fao.org/faostat/en/) data on emissions and sinks in the land use and land change (LULC) sector was used to supplement the EDGAR emissions data due to the fact that the LULC sector makes up such a significant portion of emissions from food systems. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43016-021-00225-9). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The source also includes data broken down into various disaggregations. These include disaggregation by food system stage (e.g., production, processing, distribution, consumption, end of life, etc.) and economic sector (e.g., energy, industry, land-based, and waste). ### Overview The Population Exposed to Unhealthy Levels of Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) dataset shows the percentage of a country’s population living in places with unhealthy levels of PM2.5 in the air. Particulate matter (PM) are air pollutants such as dirt, dust, soot or smoke. The [EPA categorizes](https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/particulate-matter-pm-basics) PM by size. Pollutants that are 10 micrometers or smaller in diameter can be inhaled by humans and can be harmful to human health. Fine particulate matter (less than 2.5 micrometers in diameter) poses a greater health risk than PM10. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines state that ambient air concentrations exceeding 10 micrograms of PM2.5 per cubic meter (m3) are unhealthy. Estimates of annual PM2.5 concentrations were generated by combining data from atmospheric chemistry transport models, satellite observations of aerosols in the atmosphere and ground-level particulate monitoring. These estimates were then overlain with gridded population data. This data was collected globally at the country level for select years between 1990 and 2017. PM2.5 occurs in many shapes and chemical compositions. Some particulates are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites or smokestacks. Others are created from complex reactions in the atmosphere. Cooking and heating with solid fuel sources, such as coal, wood or dung, creates harmful smoke and particulate matter. Around 40% of the world’s population relies on solid fuels for cooking and heating. The small size of PM2.5 allows particulates to get deep into the lungs and even into the bloodstream. [Scientific studies](https://www.thelancet.com/gbd?source=post_page) have linked particulate pollution exposure to various health problems including lung cancer, heart disease and respiratory disease. People with heart or lung diseases, children, and older adults are most likely to be affected by particulate pollution exposure. The [Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study](http://www.healthdata.org/gbd/2019) estimates that air pollution causes 6.5 million deaths every year. PM2.5 also negatively affects the environment causing haze, acid rain and damage to sensitive forests or farm crops. Additionally, air pollution can hinder development for low and middle-income countries and vulnerable populations. This dataset is part of the GBD study, an international scientific effort led by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation at the University of Washington. The World Bank Group commissioned the first GBD study as part of its 1993 World Development Report. The GBD believes that everyone deserves to live a long, healthy life. Their study aims to help achieve this by providing a dataset to improve health systems and eliminate disparities. A consortium of more than 3,600 researchers from more than 145 countries contributed to the GBD study. The WHO was a major contributor as well. The study quantifies the health effects of diseases and injuries and analyzes the risk factors for death and disease. Air quality is among the study’s 84 environmental, behavioral, occupational and metabolic risk factors. ### Methodology This dataset was derived from a gridded model of air quality and population. Estimates of annual PM2.5 concentration were generated by combining data from three sources: atmospheric chemistry transport models, [satellite observations of aerosols](http://fizz.phys.dal.ca/~atmos/martin/?page_id=140) in the atmosphere, and ground-level particulate monitoring. [Harvard University’s GEOS Chem](http://acmg.seas.harvard.edu/geos/) atmospheric chemistry model was used to simulate atmospheric transport of chemical air pollutants such as organic carbon, nitrate, sulfate, ammonium and mineral dust. Atmospheric aerosol observations collected by National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) satellites were combined with the GEOS Chem model to estimate atmospheric particulate concentration. Data was available at a resolution of 0.1 degrees (°). Ground-level particulate monitoring data for PM10 and PM2.5 concentrations were also used. This data was measured by 9,960 ground monitors in 108 countries. Air quality data from each of the three measurements was calibrated by country and modeled using a hierarchical statistical method. The GBD used high resolution population data from NASA’s [Gridded Population of the World](https://beta.sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu/data/collection/gpw-v4) (GPW) dataset. The GPW data was upscaled from its resolution of 0.0417° to fit the GBD’s model grid cell sizes of 0.1°. GPW data was then overlaid with gridded PM2.5 estimates to determine the percentage of a country’s population living in an area with unhealthy air quality. The WHO’s definition of unhealthy air quality are air concentrations greater than 10 micrograms of PM2.5 per m3. In grid cells where PM2.5 concentrations exceeded this threshold, the population data was summed and divided by the country’s total population. The data from all grid cells was aggregated by population-based weighted averaging to calculate each country’s population percentage figure. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(18)32225-6/fulltext#supplementaryMaterial) (supplementary appendix 1, page 67). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. ### Overview Gross domestic product (GDP) is a key economic indicator that measures the monetary value of goods and services provided within that area. The gridded GDP dataset used national GDP, gridded population data, and other factors to estimate GDP at a 30 arc-second resolution for 1990, 2000 and 2015. This gridded GDP dataset is important because it can be used for research at the sub-national level. GDP measurements are in purchasing power parity (PPP) in 2011 U.S. dollars. The data was created at Aalto University. The authors also created the [GDP per capita](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/soc073a) dataset. ### Methodology To create a high resolution, complete picture of GDP, the author first calculated GDP per capita using the World bank Development Indicators database. For missing countries, they used data from the Central Intelligence Agency World Factbook. The temporal coverage of both the national and sub-national data varied considerably. To fill in the missing values, temporal interpolation and extrapolation approaches were used. To be consistent between the sub-national and national datasets, and to ensure the data set would represent official national statistics, the authors did not use the sub-national GDP per capita directly, but instead used the sub-national data to scale national GDP per capita. This was done for each year by first calculating population-weighted national GDP per capita from sub-national GDP per capita data and the HYDE 3.2 population data set. This output was then used in each sub-national unit to calculate the ratio between population-weighted national GDP and reported sub-national GDP. The final sub-national GDP per capita (in PPP) was calculated by multiplying the ratio with the reported national GDP per capita. Reported sub-national data were used preferentially, followed by interpolated and extrapolated sub-national data, together with national averages. To estimate the total GDP of each grid cell, the authors multiplied the GDP per capita by grid specific population data using two different spatial resolutions: 5 arc-minutes (10 km at equator) and 30 arc-seconds (1 km at equator). Lower resolution population data were taken from HYDE 3.2 which includes annual data for the year 1990 and for the years 2000-2015 with a resolution of 5 arc-min. Thus, for the years 1991-1999 they needed to use the interpolated population between 1990 and 2000. Higher resolution population data were adapted from the Global Human Settlement (GHS) population grid which has data for the years 1990, 2000 and 2015 with a resolution of 30 arc-seconds. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data on GDP per capita and Human Development Index are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

The "Terrestrial Protected Areas (% of Total Land Area)" data set was published on the World Bank's open access data portal. It was created using data from the UN Environment Programme and the World Conservation Monitoring Centre and compiled by World Resources Institute. Terrestrial protected areas are defined in this instance as "totally or partially protected areas of at least 1,000 hectares that are designated by national authorities as scientific reserves with limited public access, national parks, natural monuments, nature reserves or wildlife sanctuaries, protected landscapes, and areas managed mainly for sustainable use." Marine areas, unclassified areas, littoral (intertidal) areas, and sites protected under local or provincial law are excluded. Some sites are owned and managed by governments, others by private individuals, companies, communities, and faith groups. Currently about a 10th of the world's land surface is under some form of protected area, and the system represents a unique commitment to the future. Over the last 40 years the global protected area estate has increased from an area the size of the United Kingdom to an area the size of South America. Increasing the proportion of terrestrial and marine areas protected helps defend vulnerable plant and animal species and safeguard biodiversity. This indicator is calculated using all the nationally designated protected areas recorded in the World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA) whose location and extent is known and aggregated using a weighted average. A global protected area layer is created by combining the polygons and points recorded in the WDPA. Circular buffers are created around points based on the known extent of protected areas for which no polygon is available. Annual protected area layers are created by dissolving the global protected area layer by the known year of establishment of protected areas recorded in the WDPA. The annual protected area layers are overlaid with country/territory boundaries, coastlines, and buffered coastlines (delineating the territorial waters) to obtain the absolute coverage (in km2) of protected areas by country/territory per year from 1990 to the present. The total area of a country's/territory's terrestrial protected areas and marine protected areas in territorial waters is divided by the total area of its land areas (including inland waters) and territorial waters to obtain the relative coverage (percentage) of protected areas. ### Overview This dataset contains internationally comparable emissions data on greenhouse gasses (GHG) from 1990 to 2018. Additionally, it further shows GHG emissions for six individual economic sectors and subsectors on a global scale. The GHGs include carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons (PFCs), sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆), and nitrous oxide (N₂O). The economic sectors included in the Resource Watch map are agriculture, bunker fuels, energy, industrial processes, and land-use change/forestry, and waste. This dataset is released by the World Resources Institute (WRI) as part of the larger Climate Analysis Indicators Tools (CAIT) Climate Data Explorer. This dataset is essential to help inform policymakers, researchers, and other stakeholders on countries’ climate progress. This dataset is featured in Facebook’s newly launched [Climate Science Center](https://www.facebook.com/climatescienceinfo/). The Resource Watch team provided data processing for Facebook with the goal of demonstrating historical GHG emissions from 1990 through 2018, and Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) for select countries. Learn more about our data processing on our [GitHub](https://github.com/resource-watch/blog-analysis/tree/master/req_020_facebook_ghg_emissions). ### Methodology Country GHG emissions data were collected from respected research centers, government agencies, and international bodies. To compile the country GHG emissions dataset WRI largely relied on data reported by countries to the United Nations Framework Convention (UNFCCC). To compliment this and create a broader picture of sector level GHG emissions estimates, WRI also consulted data from three nongovernmental sources: Carbon Dioxide Information Analysis Center (of the U.S. Dept. of Energy) (CDIAC), Energy Information Administration (of the U.S. Dept. of Energy) EIA, and the International Energy Agency (IEA). The data sources were selected based on criteria like accuracy and temporal and geographic coverage ranges. Country datasets were produced by employing a consistent methodology. Sector-level GHGemissions estimates were taken from the same sources as country level GHG emission data. Additionally, emissions data onLand Use Change and Forestry (LUCF) came from the Statistics Division of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). The final product has sector level GHG emissions data available for agriculture, industrial processes, energy, bunker fuels, land use and forestry, and waste. The datasets on bunker fuels includes data on carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions. Energy and land use/forestry further includes methane (CH₄)) and nitrogen dioxide (N₂O) in their dataset. The dataset on industrial processes includes data on the three GHGs described above and hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs). The dataset on agriculture only includes CH₄ and N₂O. The final dataset is presented in tabular format at a national scale. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://cait.wri.org/docs/CAIT2.0_CountryGHG_Methods.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for historical country-level CO₂ emissions data going back to 1850, and energy sub-sector CO₂ emissions data going back to 1971 are also available from the data provider. Energy subsector data is available for building, electrical/heat, fugitive emissions, manufacturing/construction, other fuel combustion, and transportation. Global Gridded Geographically Based Economic Data (G-Econ), Version 4, provides a measure of global cell product (GCP): estimates for the amount of gross domestic product (GDP) produced in each grid cell of a 1-degree grid of the world using 2 metrics: GCP measured in the market exchange rate (MER) from local currencies into US$, and GCP measured in purchasing power parity (PPP), which adjusts country currency GCP according to the equivalent amount of US$ needed to purchase a standardized collection of goods in the country using the country's currency. GCP is defined as the gross value added by activities in a grid cell. Gross value is calculated as the total value of the outputs of local businesses providing goods and services in the grid cell, minus the value of inputs bought by those businesses. The data and methods used to calculate local added value are different for different countries, as the data available are different for different countries. State- and county level gross value data are used whenever possible. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

### Overview This dataset shows the percentage of total final energy consumption(TFEC) that comes from renewable sources in 259 countries from 1990 to present. In this dataset, renewable energy sources are defined as hydropower, solid and liquid biofuels, wind, solar, biogas, geothermal, marine, and waste to energy. The dataset was published as part of the Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) initiative, and the data was compiled by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the United Nations Statistics Divisions (UNSD). IEA and UNDC are the primary developers of internationally comparable national energy statistics. This dataset tracks the progress of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator 7.2, to advance the target of increase substantially the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix by 2030. Resource Watch also shows [renewable energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene021a-Renewable-Energy-Consumption) and [energy intensity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene029a-Energy-Intensity) data from the SE4ALL Database. ### Methodology This dataset was compiled using data from IEA and UNSD. Renewable energy consumption was divided by total final energy consumption to calculate the share of renewable energy in the total final energy consumption of each country. Renewable energy consumption was defined as the final consumption of renewables plus the amount of electricity and heat consumption estimated to have come from renewable energy sources. Total final energy consumption was defined as the sum of the final energy consumption in the transport, industry, residential, services, and other sectors. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.seforall.org/sites/default/files/l/2013/09/9-gtf_ch4.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [renewable energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene021a-Renewable-Energy-Consumption) and [energy intensity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene029a-Energy-Intensity) data from the SE4ALL Database. ### Overview This dataset includes the percentage of the population with access to electricity from 1990 to present, at the country level. The data represents electricity access in the rural population of each country. Access to electricity is crucial to improving the standard of living and is one of the most obvious indications of a country’s energy poverty status. Securing electricity services while decarbonizing power systems is a key challenge for developing countries, as electricity generation from fossil fuels contributes to climate change. While this dataset shows access to electricity at the national level, Resource Watch also shows data for the percentage of [urban](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/1ad53858-f5da-47cb-8006-5b4aa5aad589) and [national](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene012a-Access-to-Electricity) population with access to electricity. This dataset comes from a Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) database from the SE4ALL Global Tracking Framework led jointly by the World Bank, the International Energy Agency (IEA), and the Energy Sector Management Assistance Program (ESMAP). ### Methodology Electrification data is collected from industry, national surveys, and international sources. Data generally comes from nationally representative household surveys like national censuses. Survey sources include Demographic and Health Surveys (DHSs) and Living Standards Measurement Surveys (LSMSs), Multi-indicator Cluster Surveys (MICSs), the World Health Survey (WHS), other nationally developed and implemented surveys, and various government agencies (for example, ministries of energy and utilities). Given the low frequency and the regional distribution of some surveys, a number of countries have gaps in available data. To develop the historical evolution and starting point of electrification rates, a simple modeling approach was adopted to fill in the missing data points: around 1990, around 2000, and around 2010. Therefore, a country can have a continuum of 0 to 3 data points. There are 42 countries with 0 data points, and the weighted regional average was used as an estimate for electrification in each of the data periods. 170 countries have between 1 and 3 data points, and missing data are estimated by using a model with region, country, and time variables. The model keeps the original observation if data are available for any of the time periods. This modeling approach allowed the estimation of electrification rates for 212 countries over these 3 time periods (indicated as "Estimate"). The notation "Assumption" refers to the assumption of universal access in countries classified as developed by the United Nations. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. The Global Tracking Framework (GTF) provides indicators on progress made toward the SE4ALL goals to ensure universal access to modern energy services, double the global rate of improvement in global energy efficiency, and double the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix. These indicators are assembled by a coalition of partner agencies, led by the World Bank, the International Energy Agency (IEA), and the Energy Sector Management Assistance Program (ESMAP), along with more than 20 other partner agencies. For a full list, see http://gtf.esmap.org/about-us. The 2017 edition of the GTF includes the following indicators on the 3 SE4ALL goals: access to electricity for urban, rural, and total populations; primary energy intensity; and total final energy consumption; the share of renewable energy in total final energy consumption; renewable energy consumption; share of renewable energy in electricity output; total electricity output; and renewable energy electricity output. Each of these indicators has a unique methodology, all of which can be reviewed in the GTF methodology at http://gtf.esmap.org/methodology. Users are encouraged to thoroughly review the methodology for each indicator before using the contained data for planning purposes or other analyses. The CO₂ Emissions Comparison for Transit Buses was developed by World Resources Institute (WRI) using emission factors for grid electricity from Ecometrica, fuel combustion emissions data from International Energy Agency 2012 and 2013(IEA), electric power transmission and distribution loss data from the World Bank Group's World Development Indicators, and purchased electricity values from Greenhouse Gas Protocol (GHGP). The climate change impacts of electric vehicles (EV) vary globally depending on the fuel used to power the electric grid. EVs are increasingly becoming a better choice as electric grids improve efficiency and integrate more renewable energy sources. While the efficiency of the vehicle has a large impact on the operational costs, social benefits, and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, it is important to understand the energy mix from your local energy grid – as there is significant variation within countries. The data represents the ratio of CO₂ emissions from electric and diesel buses. The purpose of the data is to compare the GHG emissions of the EV and typical ICE diesel bus for the years 1990-2012 on a national level. Where the interactive Resource Watch global map is green, the emissions from the EV are lower, based on the national average energy grid, compared to the emissions from the typical ICE diesel bus. Where the interactive Resource Watch global map is red, the emissions from the EV are higher, based on the national average energy grid, compared to the emissions from the typical ICE diesel bus.

The Tracking Network uses Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) air quality monitor data to calculate Number of Days with Maximum 8-Hour Average Ozone Concentration Over the National Ambient Air Quality Standard. For each county with complete monitoring data, the data include: the year, state, county FIPS code, total county population, population with monitors, population without monitors, number of days above benchmark (default NAAQS), person-days above benchmark (default federal NAAQS). To calculate the annual number of days over the daily NAAQS, number of days with ozone levels over the daily 8-hr NAAQS for the entire year are summed. To calculate Person-days with ozone levels over the daily 8-hr NAAQS, the number of days over the daily NAAQS by the total population of the county are multiplied. EPA Air Quality Standard monitoring data, which are used in the calculation of measures, are not present for all counties and days. Since ozone levels decrease significantly in the colder parts of the year in many areas, ozone is required to be monitored only during the "ozone season." Ozone seasons are designated on a State by State basis. When creating measures, we only consider monitors with 75% completeness during the ozone season. Additionally, the data for this indicator represent only counties that have air monitors; thus the data tend to reflect urban air quality (where most people live). Although populations in areas without monitors also may be exposed to ozone that exceeds the standard, they are not counted. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. ### Overview This dataset includes the estimated unemployment rate in 208 countries from 1991 to present and is updated annually. The unemployment rate is the percentage of the labor force that is without work but available for and seeking employment. The unemployment rate is an indicator of an economy’s efficiency and effectiveness to absorb its labor force. High and consistent unemployment suggests serious inefficiencies in resource allocation. The dataset is published by the International Labour Organization (ILO), through its Department of Statistics (ILOSTAT). ### Methodology Country-level estimations of unemployment rates came from several data sources. Nationally representative labor force surveys were first consulted for this data. In the case that this survey data was not available, other sources like population censuses and nationally reported estimates were used. In cases of missing values, an ILO econometric model was used. This model ensured that data was comparable across countries and over time by accounting for differences in data sources, the scope of coverage, methodology, and other country-specific factors. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.ilo.org/ilostat-files/Documents/TEM.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. ### Overview The Employment in Agriculture (% of total employment) dataset shows national employment in agriculture as a percentage of total employment. This dataset is compiled by the World Bank Group. Data is available globally at the national level from 1991 through present. ### Methodology The Employment in Agriculture (% of total employment) dataset is compiled by the World Bank Group from the International Labour Organization ILOSTAT database. The ILO classifies economic activity using the International Standard Industrial Classification (ISIC) of All Economic Activities. Employment is defined as persons of working age who were engaged in any activity to produce goods or provide services for pay or profit, whether at work during the reference period or not at work due to temporary absence from a job, or to working-time arrangement. The agriculture sector consists of activities in agriculture, hunting, forestry and fishing. Because this classification is based on where work is performed (industry) rather than type of work performed (occupation), all of an enterprise's employees are classified under the same industry, regardless of their trade or occupation. World Bank Group uses weighted averages to aggregate sectoral information and thus account for broad shifts in employment and stages of development. In the textbook case of economic development, labour flows from agriculture and other labour-intensive primary activities to industry and finally to the services sector; in the process, workers migrate from rural to urban areas. The series is part of the ILO estimates and is harmonized to ensure comparability across countries and over time by accounting for differences in data source, scope of coverage, methodology, and other country-specific factors. The estimates are based mainly on nationally representative labor force surveys, with other sources (population censuses and nationally reported estimates) used only when no survey data are available. description: The Relative Magnitude of Fragmentation (RMF) measures the fragmentation of specific land cover types using the entropy-based local indicator of spatial association (ELSA). The values of ELSA vary between 0 and 1 (multiplied by a scale factor of 10000) denoting lowest and highest fragmentation. We use an existing spatially contiguous, global remote-sensing data product (i.e. the 27-year annual ESA CCI land cover maps which can be categorized as an EBV 'Ecosystem Distribution') to derive an annual (27 year) time-series of the Relative Magnitude of Fragmentation (RMF) at a global scale and with a spatial resolution of 300m. From this derived EBV data product, we can calculate a RMF indicator of ecosystem degradation, i.e. the change, and rate of change, in fragmentation of ecosystems (e.g. forests) over the last 27 years. This can provide important information for measuring biodiversity change as it directly links to the draft monitoring framework of the zero draft of the post-2020 global biodiversity framework of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), especially Draft 2050 Goal 1 and the related Draft 2030 Target 1 (see Annex of the zero draft). description: This data set (version 2.07) was created as part of the Climate Change Initiative (CCI), an initiative of the European Space Agency to create long-term, consistent, global data for the purposes of climate modelling. The CCI Land Cover project delivers consistent global land cover maps at 300 m spatial resolution on an annual basis from 1992 to 2015. The Global Nature Watch platform only displays the 2015 land cover data. To ensure consistency from year to year, land cover maps for each year are derived from a single baseline land cover map. The baseline map was created using the full record of MERIS images from 2003 to 2012, using unsupervised classification as well as a machine learning algorithm over multiple years of imagery. Changes are then detected between individual years at 1 km resolution, using AVHRR data from 1992 to 1999, SPOT-VGT data from 1999 to 2013, and PROVA-V data from 2014 and 2015. Changes must be consistent for two consecutive years in order to be counted, with the exception of forest changes in 2014 and 2015 which are assumed to be well detected. The 1 km changes are then combined with the baseline land cover map and delineated to 300 meters for 2004 onward (when MERIS and PROVA-V data are available). The resulting data have a total of 22 global land cover classes. For the sake of better visualization, Global Nature Watch shows only a set of simplified classes, based on the IPCC (agriculture, forest, grassland, wetland, settlement, shrubland, sparse vegetation, bare area, water, and permanent ice and snow). The full set of classes as well as annual land cover maps back to 1992 are available on the [ESA/CCI viewer](http://maps.elie.ucl.ac.be/CCI/viewer/).

description: The Defense Meteorological Satellite Program Operational Linescan System (DMSP-OLS) created the Annual Nighttime Lights: Stable Composites from 1992 until 2013 at a 30 arc second grid resolution (approximately 1 km square grids). These composites account for where light has been observed throughout an entire year. Pixels are identified as being "stable lights" when light is detected there in more than 90-94% of valid observations. The long period of observation allows the product to include observations in places that are cloudy or otherwise obscured many days of the year. This data have been shown to be correlated with regional economic development. The DMSP satellites fly in a sun-synchronous low Earth orbit (833 km mean altitude) such that they pass over any given point on Earth between 20:30 and 21:30 local time. With 14 orbits per day, each DMSP satellite provides global nighttime coverage every 24 hours. There are normally 2 satellites orbiting simultaneously, and each satellite has a lifespan of 6 to 8 years. The light intensity is measured by sensors mounted on these satellites. The observations a satellite makes of a given pixel throughout the year will be from various heights and viewing angles. A mathematical procedure is used to average all of these observations to create the annual nighttime lights product. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: Water velocity are two products from the Hybrid Coordinate Ocean Model (HYCOM), created by the HYCOM Consortium, the National Ocean Partnership Program (NOPP), and the United States Global Ocean Data Assimilation Experiment (GODEA). HYCOM is a fully three dimensional, multivariate, variational ocean data assimilation system that produces simultaneous analyses of temperature, salinity, geopotential and vector velocity. The analysis is run in real-time and updates daily. The data have been interpolated to a uniform 0.08 degree lat/long grid between 80.48°S and 80.48°N. The salinity, temperature, and velocity variables have been interpolated to 40 standard z-levels (vertical depth). The high resolution makes HYCOM eddy resolving. Eddy-resolving models can more accurately simulate western boundary currents and the associated mesoscale variability and they better maintain more accurate and sharper ocean fronts. In particular, an eddy resolving ocean model allows upper ocean topographic coupling via flow instabilities. The coupling occurs when flow instabilities drive abyssal currents that in turn steer the pathways of upper ocean currents. In ocean prediction this coupling is important for ocean model dynamical interpolation skill in data assimilation/nowcasting and in ocean forecasting, which is feasible on time scales up to about a month. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: Note: This Generation 1 Collection has been superseded by Generation 2 Simulation-level Collections The DestinE Digital Twin for Climate Change Adaptation (Climate DT) supports adaptation activities by providing innovative climate information on multi-decadal timescales, globally, at scales at which many impacts of climate change are observed. It combines cutting-edge global Earth-system models, impact-sector applications and observations into a unified framework to provide global climate projections and impact-sector information on multi-decadal timescales (1990 to ~2050), at very high spatial resolutions (5 to 10 km). The Climate DT represents the first ever attempt to operationalise the production of global multi-decadal climate projections, leveraging the world-leading supercomputing facilities of the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking along with some of the leading European climate models. A concise overview of what the Climate DT aims to achieve, and of the different concepts essential for an understanding of the Digital Twin’s characteristics, is included in the [Climate DT factsheet](https://destine.ecmwf.int/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/2024.06.07_Climate-DT-Fact-Sheet_V7-2.pdf) ## Historical Simulation Starting in 1990, the forcing follows observed changes in greenhouse gases, aerosols etc. until 2020. The simulations are using standardised CMIP6 forcing. Historical simulations are essential for model evaluation and quality control as they allow a comparison to observations. ## Models The Climate DT exploits and further evolves a new generation of global storm-resolving and eddy-rich models built through a cooperative model development approach. For more information on models please click [here](https://destine.ecmwf.int/climate-change-adaptation-digital-twin-climate-dt/#models) ## Simulations The Climate DT team carries out several types of digital twin simulations on the EuroHPC supercomputers. Multi-decadal simulations are produced to cover the recent past (from 1990) and possible future evolutions of the climate up to 2050. See [here](https://destine.ecmwf.int/climate-change-adaptation-digital-twin-climate-dt/#simulations) for more information on Simulations ## Parameters Below we see the list of parameters extracted from the 'DestinE Climate DT data portfolio', for more information please refer to the page [Climate DT Phase 1 CLTE Parameters](https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/DDCZ/Climate+DT+Phase+1+data+catalogue)

### Overview The Solar Energy Potential dataset is made up of two layers: average daily global horizontal irradiation (GHI) and average daily photovoltaic power potential. GHI is the sum of direct and diffuse radiation received on a horizontal plane presented in the units kilowatt hour per square meter (kWh/m²). Radiation is energy that moves from one place to another and in this dataset it refers to energy released by the sun traveling to Earth. Irradiance refers to the average amount of radiation received in a given area on Earth. Photovoltaic power potential, or Potential photovoltaic electricity Production (PVOUT), is the estimated amount of energy converted by a photovoltaic system into electricity presented in kilowatt-hour per kilowatt peak of the photovoltaic system (kWh/kWp) according to the geographical conditions of a site and configuration of the photovoltaic system. GHI acts as an important base measurement to help determine regions that receive enough sunlight and is used to assess an area for flat-plate photovoltaic and solar heating technologies. PVOUT works to calculate the actual effectiveness of a solar energy project in the region based on local conditions. The datasets were created using geostationary satellite imagery and meteorological models, including SolarGIS’s global solar model (v2.1). Satellite imagery data comes from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), North American Space Agency (NASA), European Organisation for the Exploitation of Meteorological Satellites (EUMESTAT), and Japan Meteorological Administration (JMA). The final averages presented in these datasets were created using yearly and daily averages taken between 1994/1999/2007 and 2018, depending on region of the world. The GHI dataset is presented on Resource Watch at a spatial resolution of 250 meters and PVOUT 1 kilometer. These datasets are taken from SolarGIS’s Global Solar Atlas, which is funded by the World Bank’s Energy Sector Management Assistance Program (ESMAP). The Global Solar Atlas was created to help companies and governments improve the efficiency of photovoltaic projects. Increasing sustainable energy production, like solar, is a crucial step in reducing the world’s reliance on fossil fuels. ### Methodology The average daily global horizontal irradiation (GHI) and average daily photovoltaic power potential layers were created using SolarGIS’s global solar model (v2.1). The model utilizes data from geostationary satellites and metrological models. First, clear-sky irradiance values were calculated using the position of the sun on earth at a given time. The irradiance values used in the calculations assumed that there were no clouds present in the sky. This determined the sun’s irradiance that reached earth based on the effect of altitude, concentration of aerosols (particles coming from different sources, natural and human), water vapor, and ozone. Then data from geostationary meteorological satellites was input to determine cloud cover during the same time period. These two data sources were coupled to provide the global horizontal irradiation values. The photovoltaic power potential was calculated by combining the horizontal irradiation dataset with data on surface air temperature and a simulation of photovoltaic power cells. First, the horizontal irradiation dataset was converted into irradiation at optimum tilt to provide ideal conditions for power potential on a photovoltaic cell. Optimum tilt refers to the most efficient angle for a surface to be at to receive the highest amount of the sun’s radiation. Surface air temperature data was collected from meteorological stations when available and otherwise from meteorological models. Data from models was disaggregated by SolarGIS to increase their spatial resolution. The photovoltaic power cell simulation used was the Single-diode equivalent circuit simulation. To create a daily average value of GHI and PVOUT, data was averaged between 1994 and 2018 for Europe/Africa, 1999 and 2018 for North America/South America/Central Asia, and 2007 and 2018 for East Asia. GHI data was presented in kWh/m² at a spatial resolution of 9 arcsec (250 m). PVOUT data was in kWh/kWp with a spatial resolution of 30 arcsec (1 km). For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for diffuse horizontal irradiation, direct normal irradiation, terrain elevation above sea level, global irradiation for optimally tilted surfaces, optimum tilt to maximize yearly yield, and air temperature at 2 m above ground level is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved and pre-processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/ene_031a_solar_irradiance). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

The Gender Inequality Index (GII), released by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), is an inequality index for 159 countries from 1995 to 2015. It measures gender inequalities and is calculated using 3 important aspects of human development: (1) reproductive health, measured by maternal mortality ratio and adolescent birth rates; (2) empowerment, measured by proportion of parliamentary seats occupied by females and proportion of adult females and males aged 25 years and older with at least some secondary education; and (3) economic status, expressed as labor market participation and measured by labor force participation rate of female and male populations aged 15 and older. The index ranges from 0, where women and men fare equally, to 1, where one gender fares as poorly as possible in all measured dimensions. The higher the GII value, the more disparities between females and males and the more loss to human development. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set.
