### Overview The University of Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative (ND-GAIN) produces an annual index that measures a country’s vulnerability to climate change along with its readiness to respond and adapt. The index assesses 192 countries annually from 1995-2019. The index is on a scale from 0-100, with higher numbers indicating that the country is better poised to respond to climate disruptions. Every country around the world will experience and respond differently to climate disruptions. Due to the unique socioeconomic and geographic locations of each country, some will be more vulnerable from the impacts of climate change and will have differing capacities to adapt. ND-GAIN’s index combines a vulnerability score with a readiness score to assess each country. Vulnerability measures a country's exposure, sensitivity, and capacity to adapt to the negative effects of climate change. Readiness measures a country's ability to leverage investments and convert them to adaptation actions. This index provides a standardized way to estimate a country's adaptation risk and opportunity. ND-GAIN is a program within the Notre Dame Environmental Change Initiative with the goal of heightening awareness and understanding of adaptation, providing products and services to spur action, and enhance investments in vulnerable communities. ### Methodology The ND-GAIN index measures both a country's vulnerability to climate change and its readiness to take adaptation actions. Vulnerability is assessed by considering six sectors: food, water, health, ecosystem services, human habitat, and infrastructure. Each sector is composed of six indicators (36 total) that relate to three components: exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity. - Exposure measures the extent to which society and its supporting sectors are stressed by future climate conditions. - Sensitivity relates to the degree to which people and the sectors they depend on are affected by climate related disturbances. - Adaptive capacity measures the ability of society to respond and decrease the negative consequences of climate related events. Similarly, readiness is assessed by three core components - economic readiness, governance readiness, and social readiness - and nine indicators to produce an overall readiness metric that gauges a country's ability to leverage investments and adaptation actions. - Economic readiness represents the investment environment which is needed to marshal funds from the private sector. - Governance readiness relates to the conditions (stability of society, institutional arrangements) that contribute to investment risk. - Social readiness measures the social conditions that enable society to make efficient and equitable use of and benefit from an investment. 74 data sources are used to construct the 45 indicators that make up the readiness and vulnerability scores. 20 indicators come directly from raw data sources, the other 25 are computed by the underlying data. The following steps outline how the index is created: 1. Collect the raw data and process 2. Interpolate missing data or denote certain indicators as “missing” for specific countries 3. Identify the baseline minimum and maximum values from the raw data 4. Define a reference point for each indicator (e.g. reference point for child malnutrition is 0%) 5. Scale the raw data to score, from 0 to 1, to allow for comparison 6. Compute the vulnerability and readiness scores 7. Compute ND-GAIN and scale scores to give a value from 0 to 100 (higher values representing greater readiness and lower vulnerability) ### Additional Information Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. The ND-GAIN dataset also includes data for each vulnerability sector (food, ecosystem services, health, human habitat, infrastructure, water), readiness sector (economic, governance, social), all 45 indicators, and trends. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. See the documentation on how we processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_029_rw2_vulnerability_to_climate_change). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

The Subnational Human Development Index (SHDI) was constructed by the Global Data Lab (GDL) at the Institute for Management Research at Radboud University (RU). The index is a measure of the average subnational values for three dimensions of subnational human development: education, health, and standard of living for the period 1995-2019. In its official version defined at the national level, these dimensions are measured with the following indicators: Education measured with the variables ‘Mean years of schooling of adults aged 25+’ and ‘Expected years of schooling of children aged 6’; health measured with ‘Life expectancy at birth’ and standard of living measured with ‘Gross National Income per capita (PPP, 2011 US$)’. This dataset was translated from the United Nations Development Programme’s (UNDP) official Human Development Index (HDI) to the subnational level using subnational values retrieved from the Area Database of the Global Data Lab, national statistical offices, and the EU statistical office (Eurostat). The Gender Development Index (GDI), published by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), measures gender gaps in human development achievements by accounting for disparities between women and men in 3 basic dimensions of human development using the same component indicators as in the Human Development Index (HDI). The HDI is a summary measure of average achievement in key dimensions of human development: a long and healthy life, being knowledgeable, and a decent standard of living. The HDI is the geometric mean of normalized indices for each of the 3 dimensions. The health dimension is assessed by life expectancy at birth; the education dimension is measured by mean of years of schooling for adults aged 25 years and more and expected years of schooling for children of school-entering age. The standard-of-living dimension is measured by gross national income per capita. The HDI uses the logarithm of income to reflect the diminishing importance of income with increasing gross national income (GNI). The scores for the 3 HDI dimension indices are then aggregated into a composite index using geometric mean. The GDI is the ratio of the HDIs calculated separately for females and males using the same methodology as in the HDI. It is a direct measure of gender gap, showing the female HDI as a percentage of the male HDI. The GDI is calculated for 161 countries in 2015 and shows how much women are lagging behind their male counterparts in each dimension of human development. It facilitates understanding of the real gender gap in human development achievements and is useful in designing policy tools to close the gap. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](4d2d47c1-fed1-4484-83e3-c91c3f6f7315) as a replacement.**_ The University of Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative (ND-GAIN) produces an annual index of climate change adaptation potential annually from 1995 to 2015. A country's ND-GAIN score is composed of a vulnerability score and a readiness score. Vulnerability and readiness are based on compiled indicators. Vulnerability measures a country's exposure, sensitivity, and capacity to adapt to the negative effects of climate change. ND-GAIN measures overall vulnerability by considering 6 life-supporting sectors—food, water, health, ecosystem service, human habitat, and infrastructure—and 36 indicators. Readiness measures a country's ability to leverage investments and convert them to adaptation actions. ND-GAIN measures overall readiness by considering 3 components—economic readiness, governance readiness, and social readiness—and 9 indicators. Each indicator comes from a public data source. ### Overview This dataset shows the global extent of mangroves for 1996, 2007, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2015 and 2016. This is the first global map of mangrove extent produced using an automated, reproducible, and globally consistent methodology, using a combination of optical and radar satellite data. Mangroves are forested intertidal ecosystems that perform critical landscape-level functions related to the regulation of freshwater, nutrients, and sediment inputs into marine areas. They play a key role in helping to control the quality of marine coastal waters. Mangroves are of critical importance as breeding and nursery sites for birds, fish, and crustaceans. Additionally, they constitute important sinks for carbon storage. Once abundant along the world’s tropical and subtropical coastlines, mangroves are in global decline. Significant drivers of change include removal for aquaculture, agriculture, energy exploitation and other industrial development, with an unknown proportion of the remaining mangroves fragmented and degraded. Mangroves are also sensitive to climate change effects such as sea level rise, temperature extremes, and changes in hydrology. The dataset has been generated by the [Global Mangrove Watch (GMW)](https://www.globalmangrovewatch.org) – a collaboration between Aberystwyth University (U.K.), solo Earth Observation (soloEO), Wetlands International, the World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). DOB Ecology supported the mapping in Africa through the Mangrove Capital Africa project. ### Methodology The mangrove maps were derived in two steps: 1) generation of a baseline map of global mangrove extent for the year 2010 and 2) detection of changes between the 2010 baseline and each of the other six years. **2010 global mangrove extent baseline map:** The 2010 baseline map was derived by the Random Forest Classification algorithm that used a combination of L-band radar (ALOS PALSAR) and optical (Landsat-5, -7) satellite data. Approximately 15,000 Landsat scenes and 1,500 ALOS PALSAR (1 x 1 degree) mosaic tiles were used to create optical and radar image composites covering the coastlines along the tropical and sub-tropical coastlines in the Americas, Africa, Asia, and Oceania. The classification was confined using a mangrove habitat mask, which defined regions where mangrove ecosystems can be expected to exist. The mangrove habitat definition was generated based on geographical parameters such as latitude, elevation, and distance from ocean water. Training for the habitat mask and classification of the 2010 mangrove mask was based on randomly sampling 38 million points using historical mangrove maps (for the year 2000) of Giri et al. (2011) and Spalding et al. (2010) and the water occurrence layer defined by Pekel et al. (2017). Classification accuracy of the 2010 baseline dataset was assessed with approximately 53,800 randomly sampled points across 20 randomly selected regions. Overall accuracy was 95.25 %, while User’s and Producer’s accuracies for the mangrove class were estimated at 97.5% and 94.0%, respectively. **1996, 2007, 2008, 2009, 2015 and 2016 maps of mangrove extent and changes:** The maps for the other six years were derived by detection and classification of losses (defined as a decrease in radar backscatter) and gains (defined as a backscatter increase) between the 2010 ALOS PALSAR data and JERS-1 SAR (1996), ALOS PALSAR (2007, 2008 & 2009) and ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 (2015 & 2016) data. The change pixels for each year in question were then added or removed from the 2010 baseline raster mask (buffered to allow detection of mangrove gains also immediately outside of the mask) to produce the new yearly extent maps. Classification accuracies of the changes were assessed with over 45,000 points, with an overall accuracy of 75.0 %. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/10/10/1669). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/for_005a_mangrove). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

description: The International Wealth Index (IWI) was constructed by the Global Data Lab (GDL) at the Institute for Management Research at Radboud University (RU). The index represents the first comparable asset-based index of a household’s economic status that can be used for low and middle income countries. The Index proves an understandable way for evaluating and comparing the situation of households, social groups, and societies among all regions of the developing world. The IWI was based on data from 2.1 million households in 97 developing counties. The database was comprised of 165 subnational surveys between 1996 and 2011 in 97 low and middle income countries. Most of the surveys were from the DHS Program and the Multiple Indicator Clusters Survey (MICS) collected by United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund (UNICEF). They are based on over 30 individual data sources produced by a variety of survey institutes, think tanks, nongovernmental organizations, international organizations, and private sector firms. The World Food Programme mobile Vulnerability Analysis and Mapping unit uses phone-based surveys to create a Food Consumption Score for regions at risk of needing food aid or market assistance. Household food consumption is best measured in kilocalories consumed, but these data are difficult to obtain at scale. The WFP mVAM uses the FCS survey to ask households which types of food they have eaten over the past 7 days. These responses are used to create the FCS, which can then be used to prioritize budgets to help high-need populations. The FCS survey is used as a proxy for actual caloric intake and diet quality. It is based on dietary diversity, food frequency, and the relative importance of different food groups. It uses a standardized and transparent methodology to allow for interregional and intertemporal comparability of survey results. The mVAM uses a mobile survey to ask households on how many of the past 7 days they have eaten various food items. Individual food items are grouped into 9 main food groups: cereals, starchy tubers, and roots; legumes and nuts; meat, fish, poultry, and eggs; vegetables (including green leaves); fruit; oils and fats; milk and dairy products; sugar/sweets; and condiments. Food group totals are calculated by summing the answers for the individual food items that comprise the group, each of which range from 0 to 7 days. These food group sums are then multiplied by a factor representing the nutritional importance of the food group. The raw FCS is calculated by summing the weighted food group scores. Standardized thresholds are recommend to classify households into 1 of 3 Food Consumption Groups (FCGs) based on their raw FCS: poor, borderline, or acceptable. Additional classification methods, using clustering techniques such as Principle Component Analysis, can be used which incorporate all of each household's survey responses to group them into 1 of 3 consumption profiles. Expert analysts can then review the 3 resulting groups and determine which represent the poor, borderline, and acceptable FCGs. These classifications can be compared with the raw FCS threshold classification technique to evaluate how well they agree. In most cases they should agree quite well. If they do not, this is motivation for additional investigation to better understand consumption dynamics in the region. The FCS can be calculated for both Comprehensive Food Security and Vulnerability Analyses (CFSVA) and Emergency Food Security Assessments (EFSA). The former are applied in situations where the WFP has a long-term presence and time to conduct detailed analyses; the latter are applied in emergency situations where information is needed immediately to direct life-saving support. A blog about mVAM's work: http://mvam.org A full discussion of the methodology used to construct the FCS is available here: http://documents.wfp.org/stellent/groups/public/documents/manual_guide_proced/wfp197216.pdf Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

description: ### Overview This dataset shows the change in the global extent of mangroves between 1996 and 2016. Comparable maps of mangrove gain and loss (corresponding to smaller timesteps) were part of the creation of the first global map of mangrove extent produced via an automated, reproducible, and globally consistent methodology, which used a combination of optical and radar satellite data. The data have an effective resolution of approximately 25 meters at the equator. Mangroves are forested intertidal ecosystems that perform critical landscape-level functions related to the regulation of freshwater, nutrients, and sediment inputs into marine areas. They play a key role in helping to control the quality of marine coastal waters. Mangroves are of critical importance as breeding and nursery sites for birds, fish, and crustaceans. Additionally, they constitute important sinks for carbon storage. Once abundant along the world’s tropical and subtropical coastlines, mangroves are in global decline. Significant drivers of change include removal for aquaculture, agriculture, energy exploitation and other industrial development, with an unknown proportion of the remaining mangroves fragmented and degraded. Mangroves are also sensitive to climate change effects such as sea level rise, temperature extremes, and changes in hydrology. The underlying mangrove extent dataset has been generated by the [Global Mangrove Watch (GMW)](https://www.globalmangrovewatch.org) – a collaboration between Aberystwyth University (U.K.), solo Earth Observation (soloEO), Wetlands International, the World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). DOB Ecology supported the mapping in Africa through the Mangrove Capital Africa project. ### Methodology The net extent change in global mangrove area from 1996 to 2016 was calculated by comparing the [global mangrove extent maps](https://data.unep-wcmc.org/datasets/45) provided by [Global Mangrove Watch (GMW)](https://www.globalmangrovewatch.org) for the corresponding years. **1996 and 2016 extent maps:** To develop the 1996 and 2016 mangrove extent maps, GMW first created a baseline map of mangroves for 2010 at a global level through a random forests classification of both Landsat sensor spectral composite data (all spectral wavebands) and Advanced Land Observing Satellite (ALOS) Phased Arrayed L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data.The classification was confined using a mangrove habitat mask, which defined regions where mangrove ecosystems can be expected to exist. The mangrove habitat definition was generated based on geographical parameters such as latitude, elevation, and distance from ocean water. Training for the habitat mask and classification of the 2010 mangrove mask was based on randomly sampling 38 million points using historical mangrove maps (for the year 2000) of Giri et al. (2011) and Spalding et al. (2010) and the water occurrence layer defined by Pekel et al. (2017). The maps for 1996 and 2016 were derived by detection and classification of losses (defined as a decrease in radar backscatter) and gains (defined as a backscatter increase) between the 2010 ALOS PALSAR data and JERS-1 SAR (1996) and ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 (2016) data. The change pixels for each year in question were then added or removed from the 2010 baseline raster mask (buffered to allow detection of mangrove gains also immediately outside of the mask) to produce the new extent maps. Classification accuracies of the changes were assessed with over 45,000 points, with an overall accuracy of 75.0%. **1996–2016 mangrove extent change map:** WRI derived the 1996 to 2016 extent change map by directly comparing the corresponding extent layers provided by GMW (rather than combining the change layers calculated by the authors). This comparison was performed by calculating the geometric intersection of the 1996 and 2016 extent layers. The intersection was erased from the 1996 extent to obtain loss polygons and erased from the 2016 extent to obtain gain polygons. For the full documentation for the 1996 and 2016 extent maps, please see the source [methodology](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/10/10/1669). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows the [mangrove extent time series](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/386314c4-ab42-47a7-b2cd-596b788e114d), which shows total mangrove forest cover, rather than change. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [GitHub](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/for_005a_mangrove). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

The Yield Gap and Potential Yield for Major Crops data set was created by EarthStat, the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment and the Land Use (UMN IonE), and the Global Environment Lab at the University of British Columbia (LUGE Lab at UBC) for 16 major crops. Yield gaps are defined as the difference between observed crop yields and the potential yield at the same location. Yield gaps were estimated by comparing observed yields to potential yields determined by identifying high-yielding areas within zones, or bins, of similar climate. To classify climates, 2 parameters, which are known to be fundamental drivers of plant growth, were used to describe a region's climate: growing degree days (GDD) and a crop soil moisture index (the ratio of actual evapotranspiration to potential evapotranspiration). For each climate zone and each crop, a table was generated containing the yield, harvest area, and latitude/longitude position information for each grid cell included in the distribution. The data were sorted from the grid cells by their yield values, ranking them from lowest to highest yield. The grid cells' respective harvest areas were then accumulated until arriving at the statistical information of interest: the mean, median, and 90th percentile yields. The percentage of a crop's harvested area was calculated to define a percentile yield value. The data draw on average of census data between 1997 and 2003 and are shown as 2000 at a 5 minute x 5 minute spatial resolution. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. ### Overview The FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index measures how restrictive foreign direct investment (FDI) is in a country. Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is an investment made by an entity in one country into another country’s business interests. FDI is particularly important in developing countries and emerging markets as it can provide capital for technology and infrastructure and create jobs for local workers. However, some countries that receive foreign investment impose restrictions on FDI. For a given country, the four main FDI restrictions in each economic sector were evaluated and scored based on how discriminatory they are to foreign investors. These restrictions are foreign equity limitations; screening and approval requirements; restrictions on foreign key personnel; and other operational restrictions. Scores range from 0 (no restrictions) to 1 (full restrictions). The scores of each sector were averaged to calculate the country’s FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index. This dataset includes FDI data from 22 economic sectors for OECD and G20 countries and is updated annually. The index captures a country’s ability to attract FDI. It can also be used to measure changes in regulatory restrictions over time and how these changes affect FDI inflow. Highly restrictive countries receive less FDI compared to less restrictive countries with similarly sized economies. FDI restrictions can be costly to governments in terms of loss of potential investments. They also increase costs in service sectors and negatively impact stocks. Studies of this dataset have shown that countries that reform FDI restrictions attract more foreign investors. FDI restrictions reform can positively impact developing countries by promoting economic growth and investment in human capital. The OECD created the FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index. The OECD is an international organization founded in 1961. The 36 member states work to shape policies that foster prosperity, equality, opportunity and well-being. ### Methodology The FDI Regulatory Restrictions Index uses data from 22 economic sectors. Economic sectors include industries like agriculture, media, electricity, transportation and financial services. Scoring for each sector was based on the following restriction types: Limits on the amount of foreign equity ownership permitted Screening and approval procedures applied to inward foreign direct investment Restrictions on the employment of foreigners as key personnel Other restrictions (e.g., land ownership, reciprocity requirements, access to local finance) Scoring was based on the discriminatory nature of a country’s measures, i.e. whether the measures applied to only foreign investors. Restrictions were evaluated on a 0 (no restrictions) to 1 (full restrictions) scale. The restrictiveness of each sector was calculated by adding the scores for each of the four types of FDI restrictions (with a maximum score of 1). A country’s FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index is the average of the scores from all 22 economic sectors. The score for **foreign equity limits** differentiated between three key thresholds: full exclusion of foreign participation, restrictions on foreign majority control and limits on full foreign ownership. The score further distinguished between start-up businesses and takeovers. If the measure only applied to takeovers, the score was reduced by half. **Screening and approval mechanisms** that applied only to foreign investors were scored based on a monetary threshold. Restrictive countries required approval of new FDI/acquisitions worth less than $100M U.S. or 50% of total equity. Less restrictive countries did not require approval of new FDI/acquisitions until they exceeded $100M U.S. or 50% of total equity. Open countries required no screening, only pre-notification from foreign investors. Restrictions on **foreign key personnel** were scored on two criteria: limitations on foreign employment and board of directors members. The OECD defines key personnel as employees in a managerial role or employees with essential technical skills. Restrictive countries did not allow employment of foreign key personnel. Less restrictive countries imposed time limits or required economic justification of foreign key personnel employment. Nationality/residence requirements for board of directors members are common. Restrictive countries required the majority of board members to be citizens. In contrast, less restrictive countries required only one board member to be a citizen. **Other restrictions** are measures that could affect the potential operations of foreign investors. These include restrictions on the following: land ownership, access to local finance, capital/profit repatriation, and establishment of local branches. Armed Conflict Location and Event Data in African and Asian States, produced by the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), give information on the specific dates and locations of political violence and protest, the types of events, the groups involved, fatalities, and changes in territorial control. Information is recorded on the battles, killings, riots, and recruitment activities of rebels, governments, militias, armed groups, protesters, and civilians, including events that occur in the context of civil wars and periods of instability, public protest, and regime breakdown. ACLED has recorded nearly 200,000 individual events, with ongoing data collection across Africa, South Asia, South East Asia, and the Middle East. These data can be used for immediate and long-term analysis and mapping of political violence and protest across developing countries through use of historical data, as well as informing humanitarian and development work in crisis and conflict-affected contexts through real-time data updates and reports. The project covers all African countries from 1997 to the present, 10 Asian countries from 2015 to the present, and Middle Eastern countries from 2017 to the present, with real-time updates. The map displays conflict and protest events for African states from 2006 through 2016 and Asian states from 2015 through 2016. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. Crop Land Area, Yield and Production - India SOURCE: Directorate of Economics and Statistics, Ministry of Agriculture, Government of India LINK: https://data.desagri.gov.in/website/crops-apy-report-web; https://www.mospi.gov.in/sites/default/files/publication_reports/manual_area_crop_production_23july08_1.pdf Overview The dataset comprises five-year averages of production (in tonnes), productivity/yield (in tonnes per hectare), and area (in hectares) for 55 major crops across India from 1997–98 to 2022–23. The information is provided at the district level, covering major seasonal time periods of each crop within each year. The yearly datasets were derived from crop-wise APY dataset (https://data.desagri.gov.in/website/crops-apy-report-web). Methodology Pre-Processing: The dataset available as excel report was processed and joined with district shapefile (recent by mid of year 2022, containing 755 districts) obtained from Survey of India website. To simplify the presentation, the raw yearly data was averaged into five-year intervals to highlight trends in crop production and acreage across each district. The periods were labelled as follows: 1995-2000 as 2000, 2001-2005 as 2005, 2006-2010 as 2010, 2011-2015 as 2015, 2016-2020 as 2020, and 2021-2023 as 2023. This approach was adopted based on feedback from stakeholder engagements. Layers of interest: Rice Area (in Hectares), Rice Production (in Tonnes), Rice Yield (in Tonnes/Hectare), Cotton Area (in Hectares), Cotton Production (in Tonnes), Cotton Yield (in Tonnes/Hectare) Seasons considered for Rice crop: Kharif, Rabi, Autumn, Summer Seasons considered for Cotton crop: Kharif, Rabi The agricultural crop year in India runs from July to June. The cropping season is divided into two main seasons: (i) Kharif and (ii) Rabi, based on the monsoon. The Kharif season occurs from June/July to September/October during the southwest monsoon. It aligns with the Asian summer monsoon and is mostly rainfed, with limited irrigation arrangements. The Rabi season lasts from October to March and is grown under irrigated conditions. The Summer and Autumn seasons are shorter and found only in a few states. The Summer season runs from February/March to April/May and is mostly grown under irrigated conditions. The Autumn season, from May/June to October, is mainly for long-duration crops like sugarcane and some vegetable crops. For rice crop, the season is followed in particular states of India that do not receive considerable rains from the Asian summer monsoon. Area, Yield, and Production Estimation Methods The methods for estimating area, yield, and production of crops follow standardized processes under India's agricultural statistical framework. 1. Area Estimation Methods 1.1. Temporarily Settled States (Land Record States) Crop area is estimated through field-to-field enumeration by a village accountant (Patwari/Karnam). The data is recorded in the Khasra register (a field-wise crop record). The area statistics are aggregated at village, tehsil, district, and state levels. 1.2. Permanently Settled States (Non-Land Record States) Establishment of Agency for Reporting Agricultural Statistics (EARAS) is used: - A random sample of at least 20% of villages is surveyed annually. - Complete enumeration is conducted within selected villages. - The process ensures coverage of all villages over five years. 1.3. Non-Reporting Areas Area estimates are derived using remote sensing technology and aerial photography. Ground truthing and validation methods are used to improve accuracy. 2. Yield Estimation Methods General Crop Estimation Surveys (GCES) The yield is estimated through scientifically designed crop-cutting experiments (CCE). The methodology is as follows: 2.1. Sampling Design Stratified Multistage Random Sampling: - Strata: Administrative divisions (tehsil/block). - Primary Sampling Units: Villages (selected randomly). - Second-Stage Sampling Units: Fields within selected villages. - Ultimate Sampling Units: Experimental plots of standard size (e.g., 5m x 5m). 2.2. Plot Selection Two fields are randomly selected per village. A random plot (e.g., 5m x 5m) is located within each field using random numbers. For row-planted crops (like cotton), longer plots (e.g., 10m x 5m) are used. 2.3. Harvesting and Recording The experimental plot is harvested before the rest of the field. The produce is: - Weighed immediately for gross yield. - Adjusted if required (e.g., driage experiments for rice). 2.4. Driage Adjustments - Rice: Driage experiments are conducted to adjust for moisture content, ensuring yields are reported as dried grain weight. - Cotton: In the case of cotton, the final produce is expressed in terms of lint after adopting ginning percentage (kapas to lint) as obtained from the ginning factories. 3. Production Estimation Methods Area and yield are multiplied to estimate production at village, district, state, and national levels. 4. Validation of the Area, Production and Yield estimates Final aggregation and validation occur at the national level by the Directorate of Economics and Statistics (DES). Production estimates are validated using: - Remote sensing data, - Historical trends, - Market and trade data, - Reports from local agricultural officers. For the full documentation, please see the source methodology at https://www.mospi.gov.in/sites/default/files/publication_reports/manual_area_crop_production_23july08_1.pdf. Visualizing the Data The data is available as district-level aggregates. By selecting a specific crop, area, production, yield statistic, and preferred season, the relevant layer is displayed with a gradient based on the 2023 crop year, ranging from yellow (for low values) to green (with darker shades representing higher values). The cursor can be dragged over districts and clicked to view the 5-yearly averaged values from 1995 to 2023. _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](01ae2fd7-b818-429f-a27e-a36c8def971a) as a replacement.**_ The Yield Gap and Potential Yield for Major Crops data set was created by EarthStat, the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment and the Land Use (UMN IonE), and the Global Environment Lab at the University of British Columbia (LUGE Lab at UBC) for 16 major crops. Yield gaps are defined as the difference between observed crop yields and the potential yield at the same location. Yield gaps were estimated by comparing observed yields to potential yields determined by identifying high-yielding areas within zones, or bins, of similar climate. To classify climates, 2 parameters, which are known to be fundamental drivers of plant growth, were used to describe a region's climate: growing degree days (GDD) and a crop soil moisture index (the ratio of actual evapotranspiration to potential evapotranspiration). For each climate zone and each crop, a table was generated containing the yield, harvest area, and latitude/longitude position information for each grid cell included in the distribution. The data were sorted from the grid cells by their yield values, ranking them from lowest to highest yield. The grid cells' respective harvest areas were then accumulated until arriving at the statistical information of interest: the mean, median, and 90th percentile yields. The percentage of a crop's harvested area was calculated to define a percentile yield value. The data draw on average of census data between 1997 and 2003 and are shown as 2000 at a 5 minute x 5 minute spatial resolution. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](2063964b-56c8-4080-b2a5-5a7710f321b9) as a replacement.**_ Vaisala created this global data set of average annual global horizontal irradiance (GHI, the key variable for photovoltaic (PV) projects, measured in W/m²) at a 2 arc minute resolution. Solar energy investors and project developers can use these data to identify regions of the world likely to have sufficient solar resources to make a solar generation facility a worthwhile investment. Vaisala is an industry leader in the solar resource assessment space. It has been at the forefront of research regarding the estimation of surface solar conditions to better understand and predict solar energy generation. In 2010, Vaisala produced the world's first high-resolution, globally consistent data set mapping the world's solar resource potential. The annual average GHI information from this data set is provided here at a 2 arc minute resolution and based on over a decade of half-hourly, high-resolution visible satellite imagery via the broadband visible wavelength channel. The values have been processed using a combination of peer-reviewed, industry-standard techniques and in-house, including a cloud-index algorithm that produces consistent results when used with the large number of satellites that must be combined to construct a global data set. Vaisala's complete global solar database includes 2 decades of hourly estimates of GHI, direct normal irradiance (DNI), and diffuse irradiance (DIF) and is regularly maintained and updated across 5 different versions of the data set. GHI is most relevant for fixed-panel PV installations, and DNI is most relevant for concentrated solar power (CSP) projects and PV tracking systems. This data set can be used for rapid prospecting for solar energy generation sites or conducting national or regional infrastructure, policy, or transmission planning. However, the development of specific utility-scale projects generally requires additional site-specific research after this step. The global solar data set is intended as a tool to help narrow the focus of project developers and investors to accelerate the growth of solar energy worldwide. The data set has been validated against nearly 200 publicly available ground stations around the world. description: ### Overview The Conflict and Protest Events dataset displays the dates, actors, types of violence, locations, and fatalities of all reported political violence and protest events across Africa, South and Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. Political violence and protest includes events that occur in the context of civil wars and periods of instability, public protest, and regime breakdown. This data can be used for immediate and long-term analysis and mapping of political violence and protest across developing countries through the use of historical data, as well as to inform humanitarian and development work in crisis- and conflict-affected contexts through real-time data updates and reports. This data is produced by the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED). The project covers all African countries from 1997 to the present, and select countries in the Middle East, Asia, and Europe from 2010 or 2018. ### Methodology ACLED data was coded by a range of experienced researchers, who collected information primarily from secondary source information and applied the guidelines outlined in the codebook to extract information from news reports. ACLED data was collected each week after individual researchers had scrutinized the information from reports; it was then aggregated and revised by the first coding reviewer and investigated and cross-checked by the second reviewer. The third and final reviewer inspected event notes and details. For full documentation, please read the source [methodology](https://www.acleddata.com/resources/general-guides/). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](10b47089-6457-48b4-a955-60f4f964e0f2) as a replacement.**_ The foreign direct investment (FDI) Regulatory Restrictiveness Index, released by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), measures the restrictiveness of a country’s foreign direct investment (FDI) rules by looking at the 4 main types of restrictions: (1) foreign equity limitations; (2) discriminatory screening or approval mechanisms; (3) restrictions on the employment of foreigners as key personnel; and (4) other operational restrictions, for example, restrictions on branching and on capital repatriation or on land ownership by foreign-owned enterprises. Restrictions are evaluated on a 0 (no restrictions) to 1 (full restrictions) scale. Each restriction will be given a score based on an assessment of its importance. The overall restrictiveness index is the weighted average of sectoral scores. The discriminatory nature of measures, such as when they apply to foreign investors only, is the central criterion for scoring a measure. State ownership and state monopolies, to the extent they are not discriminatory toward foreigners, are not scored. This data set contains 62 countries across 22 sectors and is currently available for the following years: 1997, 2003, 2006, and 2010-2016. For OECD and non-OECD countries who are adherents to the OECD Declaration on International Investment and Multinational Enterprises, information is collected based on countries’ lists of exceptions to national treatment. For the non-OECD countries, information is collected through investment policy reviews. Information is updated on a yearly basis following the OECD Freedom of Investment monitoring of investment measures. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. The Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) is a proxy to quantify the vegetation amount. It is defined as NDVI=(NIR-Red)/(NIR+Red) where NIR corresponds to the reflectance in the near infrared band, and Red to the reflectance in the red band. It is closely related to FAPAR and is little scale dependant. Every 10-days estimates are available at global scale in the spatial resolution of about 1km from April 1998 to 2013 based upon SPOT/VEGETATION data and from 2014 to 2020 based upon PROBA-V data

We recommend using [this dataset](ef9945f7-d934-4a88-a02a-570f14fffefc) as a replacement.**_ Global Report on Internal Displacement, created by the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC), provides data on the number of internally displaced persons (IDPs) due to conflict, violence, and natural disasters worldwide. IDPs suffer from the forced nature of displacement within internationally recognized borders. Broadly, IDPs include people who have been forced to flee the source of their livelihoods, such as pastoralists who have left their grazing lands. They also include nonnationals such as migrants, asylum seekers, or stateless people who are displaced by violence or conflict inside a country, and former refugees who have returned to their home country but have not been able to go back to their habitual place of residence. These data can be used to manage resources to assist IDPs in 1) finding temporary housing and 2) establishing a sustainable living situation away from the conflict affecting their original homes or in the aftermath of a disaster event. To collect and disseminate data, the IDMC partnered with the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), and the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), as well as country governments, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) and national Red Cross and Red Crescent societies, nongovernmental organizations, and international media outlets. Data from multiple sources were cross-referenced with each other geographically and temporally to account for biases or double-counting in the reported figures. The total IDPs represent cumulative totals from decades of past conflict through December 31, 2016. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. Vaisala created this global data set of average annual wind speeds at 80 m above the Earth's surface, a common height for wind turbines when the data set was originally created in 2008. The map resolution is 2 arc minutes and average wind speeds are measured in m/s. These data can be used to identify regions of the world likely to have sufficient wind resources to make wind energy generation a worthwhile investment. Vaisala pioneered the use of numerical weather prediction (NWP) models for producing realistic wind flows around the world to better understand and predict wind energy generation. NWP models are physically based and use powerful supercomputers to simulate the interaction between the entire atmosphere and the Earth's surface, even in places where no direct observations are available. This methodology captures the myriad processes responsible for wind—from jet-level dynamics to surface-level processes—and creates a more robust and accurate wind climatology. In essence, the models use numerical methods to obtain approximate answers to mathematical equations that describe the physics and dynamics of the atmosphere. To solve these equations for different locations on the globe, the atmosphere is divided into many small elements, both horizontally and vertically. The model computes what happens within each model element and how much mass, energy, and momentum is exchanged between the model elements. In 2008, with the release of its global wind data set, Vaisala was the first to map global wind potential at high resolution by using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model and conducting a 10-year computer simulation at a 2 arc minute (approximately 5 km) resolution. This data set can be used for rapid prospecting for wind energy generation sites or conducting national or regional infrastructure, policy, or transmission planning. However, the development of specific utility-scale projects requires additional site-specific research after this step. The global wind data set is intended as a tool to help to narrow the focus of project developers and investors to accelerate the growth of wind energy worldwide. The data set was validated against publicly available wind speed observations from more than 4,000 globally distributed meteorological stations from the National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP) Automated Data Processing (ADP) surface observations data set. For more validation information, please visit http://www.vaisala.com/en/energy/Documents/WEA-ERG-3TIER-Global%20Wind%20Dataset.pdf. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. Increased mortality is associated with increased heat. Climate change is projected to increase the number of heat related deaths. As such, tracking the number of heat related deaths may help public health professionals design targeted adaptation and response options for their specific regional requirements. The Heat-Related Mortality: Number of summertime (May-Sep) heat-related deaths by year is derived by the Center for Disease Control and Prevetnion's (CDC) Environmental Health Tracking Branch using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data with appropriate ICD-10 codes to calculate the total number of deaths by year during summer (May - September) period by year for the United States. Deaths from excessive heat exposure are defined based on codes from the tenth revision of International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10). Such deaths included those in which exposure to excessive natural heat (code X30) was reported as either the underlying or a contributing cause of death. Deaths due to exposure to excessive heat of man-made origin (W92) were excluded. Blanks or missing data within the maps, tables, and charts may be due to one of the following reasons: (1) data were not collected, (2) data were collected but were not provided to CDC, or (3) data were incomplete or did not meet data quality standards.

Potential Natural Vegetation is a data set created by EarthStat to identify what vegetation would be most likely to exist now in the absence of human activities. In regions not dominated by human land use, the vegetation types are those currently observed from a satellite. This differs from presettlement natural vegetation to the extent that vegetation types have changed because of changing environmental conditions such as climate and CO₂ concentrations. 1 km resolution DISCover data were classified under the Olson Global Ecosystems (OGE) framework to derive the potential vegetation data set. First the 94 OGE classes were reclassified into 15 potential vegetation types and 3 additional classes: land use, wetlands, and water. Wetlands are poorly characterized in the DISCover data and were thus ignored; only upland natural vegetation was considered. Each 5 minute resolution grid cell was searched among the 1 km pixels for the dominant potential upland vegetation class and was assigned to be the potential vegetation. Some grid cells had 2 dominant potential vegetation classes, or none. In these cases, the search was iterated to the adjacent 1 km pixels until a dominant potential vegetation class was found. The questionnaires are based on international standards, classifications, and measures that are regularly reviewed and modified by the UIS in order to address emerging statistical issues and improve the quality of data. The UIS collaborates with the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and Eurostat to collect data with surveys (collectively UOE). The UOE questionnaire compiles data from high- and middle-income countries that are members or partner countries of the OECD or Eurostat. The UOE survey gathers more detailed education statistics. Midyear population estimates for countries with at least 90,000 inhabitants are provided by the UN Population Division to calculate the percentages. description: ### Overview This dataset shows “significant wave height," a measure for wave height that closely corresponds to what a trained observer would consider to be the mean wave height. More precisely, it is the average of the highest one-third of waves (measured from trough to crest) that occur in a given period. This is measured because the larger waves are usually more significant than the smaller waves. For instance, the larger waves in a storm cause the most beach erosion, or can cause navigation problems for mariners. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)/National Weather Service (NWS)/National Centers for Environmental Protection (NCEP) generate operational ocean wave predictions four times a day, and include 9-, 6- and 3-hour hindcasts, forecasts of every hour from the initial time out to 120 hours, and then forecasts at 3-hour intervals out to 180 hours. All outputs are global in scope, with 30-arc minute spatial resolution. ### Methodology WAVEWATCH III is a community wave modeling framework that includes the latest scientific advancements in the field of wind-wave modeling and dynamics. The core of the framework consists of the WAVEWATCH III third-generation wave model, developed at the US National Centers for Environmental Prediction in the spirit of the WAM model. The current framework evolved from earlier WAVEWATCH I & II model packages, and differs from its predecessors in many important points such as governing equations, model structure, numerical methods and physical parameterizations. The model considers the effects of a wide range of factors and dynamics. Inputs can include water temperature, water depth, oceanic currents, wind, and tides; the model itself also incorporates complex physical interactions, such as between water and the sea floor, between waves and other waves, and dissipation due to whitecapping, bottom friction, and surf-breaking, as well as dampening from mud or ice. The predictions presented here, such as significant wave height, use the wave model WAVEWATCH III® using operational NCEP products as input. The model is run four times a day: 00Z, 06Z, 12Z, and 18Z. WAVEWATCH III solves the random phase spectral action density balance equation for wavenumber-direction spectra. The implicit assumption of this equation is that properties of the medium (water depth and current) as well as the wave field itself vary on time and space scales that are much larger than the variation scales of a single wave. The model includes options for shallow-water (surf zone) applications, as well as wetting and drying of grid points. Propagation of a wave spectrum can be solved using regular (rectilinear or curvilinear) and unstructured (triangular) grids, individually or combined into multi-grid mosaics. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://github.com/NOAA-EMC/WW3/wiki/Manual). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Every model run includes forecasts (and hindcasts) for a large number of time periods in the following several days (and the preceding day). Furthermore, every model run generates results for many indicators: significant wave height, peak wave period, wind sea wave height and period, primary swell wave height and period, secondary swell wave height in period, as well as wind speed and direction. description: High resolution maps resulting from a trend analysis conducted for the period 2000–2020 on the probability of occurrence maps prepared by Bonannella et al. (2022). For this analysis we selected the realized distribution time series layers at 30m spatial resolution for 6 out of 16 species described in the mentioned publication: Silver fir (Abies alba Mill.) European beech (Fagus sylvatica L.) Norway spruce (Picea abies L.) Black pine (Pinus nigra J. F. Arnold) Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris L.) Common oak (Quercus robur L.) The trend analysis was conducted per pixel on each of these species individually. We fitted simple OLS regression models with the probability of occurrence as the dependent variable and time as the independent variable. After the model fitting, we also calculated the t-test statistics to determine the presence of an increasing (positive) or decreasing (negative) trend or no trend at all. By combining the regression slope coefficient (β) and the p-value from the t-test statistics we assigned each pixel to one of three classes: positive: β > 0.25 AND p-value < 0.05 negative: β < −0.25 AND p-value < 0.05 no trend / stable: −0.25 ≤ β ≥ 0.25 OR p-value > 0.05 We then aggregated the resulting classes at 1km resolution maps to capture the prevalent trend in probability of occurrence over a certain area. Files are named according to the following naming convention, e.g.: veg_abies.alba_slope_30m_0..0cm_epsg3035_v1.0 with the following fields: theme: e.g. veg, species code: e.g. abies.alba, variable name: e.g. slope, resolution in meters e.g. 30m, reference depths (vertical dimension): e.g. 0..0cm, coordinate system: e.g. epsg3035, data set version: e.g. v1.0. For each species here we provide the following layers: veg_abies.alba_slope: slope coefficient (scaling factor: 10000) veg_abies.alba_pvalue: p-value (scaling factor: 1000) veg_abies.alba_pos.trends_30m: pixels classified as positive on the original maps at 30m resolution (boolean layer with range 0–100, only the two extremes values are present) veg_abies.alba_pos.trends_1km: proportion of pixels of the positive class over a 1×1 km area (range 0–100) veg_abies.alba_neg.trends_30m: pixels classified as negative on the original maps at 30m resolution (boolean layer with range 0–100, only the two extremes values are present) veg_abies.alba_neg.trends_1km: proportion of pixels of the negative class over a 1×1 km area (range 0–100) veg_abies.alba_no.trends_30m: (pixels classified as no trend / stable on the original maps at 30m resolution (boolean layer with range 0–100, only the two extremes values are present) veg_abies.alba_no.trends_1km: proportion of pixels of the no trend / stable class over a 1×1 km area (range 0–100) Files are provided as GeoTIFFs and projected in the Coordinate Reference System ETRS89 / LAEA Europe (= EPSG code 3035). Styling files are provided in QML format A publication describing, in detail, all processing steps is currently in review. See at: Bonannella, C., Parente, L., de Bruin, S. and Herold, M. (2023). Multi-decadal trend analysis and forest disturbance assessment of European tree species: concerning signs of a subtle shift, PREPRINT (Version 1) available at Research Square [https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-3288937/v1]

The Annual Visible Night Light (VNL) V2 (VIIRS) images at 500-m spatial resolution for the period 2012 to 2021 (Elvidge et al., 2021) have been used to extrapolate the values backwards for years 2000–2011. This was done by fitting a logistic regression (per pixel) and then predicting the values for the previous years (see nightlights_stack_500m.R). After consistent time-series have been produced, I also derived the difference between average of the years 2020/2021 and years 2000/2021 (nightlights.difference_viirs.v21_m_500m_s_2000_2021_go_epsg4326_v20230318.tif): this shows average rate of change for the 22 years period. Use with caution: extrapolation of values can lead to artifacts. For most of the land surface, however, it appears that the growth of night lights follows exponential growth function and hence nights in the past can be represented accurately by fitting decay / logistic regression function. Original values from the Annual VNL V2 product have been converted from 0–200 to 0–2000 scale and are available as Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs. To cite the Annual VNL V2, please use: Elvidge, C. D., Zhizhin, M., Ghosh, T., Hsu, F. C., & Taneja, J. (2021). Annual time series of global VIIRS nighttime lights derived from monthly averages: 2012 to 2019. Remote Sensing, 13(5), 922. https://doi.org/10.3390/rs13050922 Historic night light images are also available (but at a much coarser spatial resolution) from: Li, X., Zhou, Y., Zhao, M., & Zhao, X. (2020). A harmonized global nighttime light dataset 1992–2018. Scientific data, 7(1), 168. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-020-0510-y

CSIRO Bioclimatic Ecosystem Resilience Index (BERI) is a global 30 arc-second product provided annually for 2000-2024. BERI measures the capacity of natural ecosystems to retain species diversity in the face of climate change, as a function of ecosystem area, connectivity and integrity. The indicator assesses the extent to which any given spatial configuration of natural habitat across a landscape will promote or hinder climate-induced shifts in biological distributions. It does this by analyzing the functional connectivity of each grid-cell of natural habitat to areas of habitat in the surrounding landscape which are projected to support a similar assemblage of species under climate change to that currently associated with the cell of interest. The indicator can then be aggregated and reported by any desired spatial unit – e.g. an ecosystem type, a country, or the entire planet. Regional values are obtained by aggregating with the csiro_denominator weights layer. From: https://doi.org/10.25919/bbp6-a192

CSIRO Biodiversity Habitat Index (BHI) is a global 30 arc-second product provided annually for 2000-2024. BHI estimates the level of species diversity expected to be retained within any given spatial reporting unit (e.g., a country, a broad ecosystem type, or the entire planet) as a function of the unit’s area, connectivity and integrity of natural ecosystems across it. Results for the indicator can either be expressed as 1) the ‘effective proportion of habitat’ remaining within the unit – adjusting for the effects of the condition and functional connectivity of habitat, and of spatial variation in the species composition of ecological communities (beta diversity); or 2) the effective proportion of habitat that can be translated, through standard species-area analysis, into a prediction of the proportion of species expected to persist (i.e. avoid extinction) over the long term. Regional values are obtained by aggregating with the csiro_denominator weights layer. From: https://doi.org/10.25919/bbp6-a192

CSIRO weights layer (denominator) used for the regional aggregation of the BILBI indicators (BHI, BERI, PARC-representativeness, PARC-connectedness and ecosystem condition). From: https://doi.org/10.25919/bbp6-a192

CSIRO ecosystem condition is a global 30 arc-second product provided annually for 2000-2024. It provides the ecosystem condition data used as an input to the BILBI indicators BHI, BERI and PARC-connectedness. Regional values are obtained by aggregating with the csiro_denominator weights layer. From: https://doi.org/10.25919/bbp6-a192

CSIRO Protected Area Representativeness Index (PARC: Representativeness) is a global 30 arc-second product provided annually for 2000-2024. The Protected Area Representativeness and Connectedness (PARC) indices measure the extent to which terrestrial protected areas, and other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs), are ecologically representative, and well-connected (both to one another, and to other areas of intact natural ecosystems in the surrounding landscape). This collection holds the representativeness index; connectedness is in csiro_parc_connectedness. Regional values are obtained by aggregating with the csiro_denominator weights layer. From: https://doi.org/10.25919/bbp6-a192

CSIRO Protected Area Connectedness Index (PARC: Connectedness) is a global 30 arc-second product provided annually for 2000-2024. The Protected Area Representativeness and Connectedness (PARC) indices measure the extent to which terrestrial protected areas, and other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs), are ecologically representative, and well-connected. This collection holds the connectedness index, which measures how well-connected protected areas and OECMs are, both to one another and to other areas of intact natural ecosystems in the surrounding landscape. Representativeness is in csiro_parc. Regional values are obtained by aggregating with the csiro_denominator weights layer. From: https://doi.org/10.25919/bbp6-a192

Consensus land cover dataset containing 12 data layers, each of which provides consensus information on the prevalence of one land-cover class. All data layers contain unsigned 8-bit values and the valid values range from 0-100, representing the consensus prevalence in percentage. All data layers have a spatial extent from 90ºN - 56ºS and from 180ºW - 180ºE, and have a spatial resolution of 30 arc-second per pixel (~1 km per pixel at the equator).

MapBiomas is a multi-institutional initiative to generate annual land cover and land use maps for all of Brazil using automatic classification processes applied to satellite images in Google Earth Engine. More than 20 organizations are collaborators on the project. The displayed data comes from Collection 2.3, and shows land cover and land use annually for the period 2000 to 2016. Experts map land cover and land use for each Brazilian biome individually (Amazon, Cerrado, Caatinga, Atlantic Forest, Pampa, and Pantanal) and then combine the maps with cross-cutting mapping on agriculture, pasture, urban infrastructure and the coastal zone. All processing is done on Landsat images within the collaborative MapBiomas Workspace app created by the project to run Google Earth Engine. The process uses a Random Forest classifier to group pixels into classes, with spatial and temporal filters to remove spurious pixels and impossible land use transitions between years. More detailed methodology for each biome and theme is available [here]( http://mapbiomas.org/pages/methodology). Maps and statistics of land cover and use change are presented for different periods (2000-2016, 2000-2001, etc.) on the MapBiomas portal. All data is available for download at the website of the project and maps are also available as assets to be used directly at Google Earth Engine platform. Learn more: [http://mapbiomas.org](http://mapbiomas.org) or send inquiries to [contato@mapbiomas.org]( contato@mapbiomas.org)

description: This data set provides a spatially-explicit overview of the annual planted area of soybean cultivation across South America’s agricultural frontiers, as described in Song et. al. (2021). Data is available annually from 2000 to 2019 at a 30m spatial resolution for the following biomes: Amazonia, Atlantic Forest, Caatinga, Cerrado, Chaco, Chiquitania, Pampas, and Pantanal. Song et. al. (2021) integrates long-term satellite imagery with three years of continent-wide field observations to produce annual maps of soybean cultivation. Researchers collected Landsat and MODIS imagery for November 1 through April 30 of each growing season and created 16-day time-series with phenological metrics. These metrics were combined with data on elevation, slope, and aspect and training data from 225 sampling areas to develop soybean probability maps for each year. The field observations were then used to assess the accuracy of the resulting maps, which are constrained to match the areas of field observations. This dataset addresses the absence of long-term, consistent government statistics by expanding the spatial and temporal scope of previous maps of soybean cultivation. The maps and workflow described in Song et. al. (2021) provides key historical baseline information for tracking commodity-driven deforestation and highlights emerging hotspots of soybean expansion.

description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](e00ed8ca-ee7a-4539-b6b5-0bf2c30ee0d8) as a replacement.**_ This data set, a collaboration between the Global Land Analysis and Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland, Google, the U.S. Geological Survey, and NASA, displays tree cover over all global land (except for Antarctica and a number of Arctic islands) for the year 2000 at 30 × 30 m resolution. This layer displays all vegetation greater than 5 m in height with >30% canopy density. Data in this layer were generated using multispectral satellite imagery from the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus (ETM+) sensor. The clear surface observations from over 600,000 images were analyzed using Google Earth Engine, a cloud platform for Earth observation and data analysis, to determine per pixel tree cover using a supervised learning algorithm. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

### Overview The Tree Cover dataset measures areas of tree cover in 2000. Tree cover is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters (m) in height and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. The dataset has a spatial resolution of 1 arc second which is approximately 30 m × 30 m at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Forests provide a wide range of ecosystem services that are [critical to biodiversity richness, climate regulation, carbon storage, and water supplies](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/309/5734/570?ijkey=493d3bb49264119aa5ed9175119f7e221b2093d6&keytype2=tf_ipsecsha). They provide shelter to a variety of wildlife species and supply humans with [essential products including lumber, paper, and firewood]( https://www.fs.fed.us/forestmanagement/products/#:~:text=Forest%20products%20include%20materials%20derived,nuts%2C%20and%20other%20natural%20products). In the global fight against climate change, the forest ecosystem is playing an incredibly important role since it [absorbs and stores large amounts of carbon](https://www.undp.org/content/undp/en/home/blog/2018/Forests-A-natural-solution-to-climate-change-crucial-for-a-sustainable-future.html). Through measuring the tree cover density of global forests, this dataset provides decision makers with a consistent basis on which to understand the [causes of tree cover loss](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/342/6160/850). It also helps to quantify other critical environmental issues, such as the economic drivers of [natural forest conversion to more intensive land uses](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1549-0831.1998.tb00691.x) and the effectiveness of [protected areas around the globe](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02422) to represent species diversity. The dataset was created through a collaboration among the Global Land Analysis & Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland (UMD), Google, United States Geological Survey (USGS), and National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) with the aim to provide a spatially and temporally detailed quantification of global forest change. ### Methodology The data was generated using multispectral satellite imagery from three sources: the Landsat 5 thematic mapper, the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager sensors. [Images captured during growing seasons](https://doi.org/10.14358/PERS.70.3.313) were used since they are more appropriate for mapping land cover. More than 1 million satellite images were processed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval and 400,000 Landsat 5, 7 and 8 images for the 2011-2019 interval. The following steps were taken to pre-process the images: 1. Pixel values were recalculated if image resolutions were changed. 2. Images were screened for clouds, shadows and water. 3. Images were [calibrated and normalized](http://gsp.humboldt.edu/OLM/Courses/GSP_216_Online/lesson4-1/radiometric.html) to make them comparable with one another. Land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled with a supervised learning algorithm, which involved [using labeled data to develop a machine learning model](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/problem-framing/cases#what-is-supervised-learning) to identify per pixel tree cover. To facilitate processing, each continent was characterized individually: North America, South America, Eurasia, Africa, and Australia using [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/), a cloud platform for earth observation data analysis that combines a public data catalog with a large-scale computational facility capable of handling large volumes of geospatial data. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [Tree Cover Loss](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5c5e654e-182b-4ab4-8a3c-edff79cc68ea) and [Tree Cover Gain](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/426fe3f0-12de-4adb-b3aa-850eb04f75b4) from the same dataset. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the reference multispectral imagery from 2000 and 2019 is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/for_001_rw2_tree_cover). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

The Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) National Environmental Public Health Tracking Network (EPHTN) provides the (Smoothed) Crude Rate of Hospitalization for Asthma per 10,000 Population, so that it can be used to assess the burden of asthma, monitor trends over time, identify high risk groups, and inform prevention, evaluation and program planning efforts. The development of a standardized analytic method for asthma hospital admissions among residents in each state will inform multiple users at the national, state, and local levels. The hospital data shown here are provided by state and/or local public health departments to the National Environmental Public Health Tracking Program. Data are based on the date of admission rather than the date of discharge. Hospital admission records are selected using primary diagnosis codes. These data represent number of admissions rather than number of individuals admitted to the hospital. The CDC Tracking Network suppresses data for counties with non-zero counts less than 6 and population less than 100,000 to protect confidentiality. Admissions of residents to out-of-state hospitals are excluded for most states. Admissions for border counties may be under estimated. The inclusion of these admissions by some states can affect state to state comparability. Rates were age-adjusted by the direct method using 2000 US standard population. These data are smoothed. Smoothing borrows information from neighboring areas to stabilize results from sparsely populated areas. Smoothing is used to reduce variability in the data, allowing patterns to emerge. The results for any single county should not be interpreted. Instead, use the map to identify patterns across the state or country. Data on counties designated as 'unstable', or counties corresponding with relative standard error greater than 30%, have been excluded in this visualization. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations includes global country-level statistics for areas of forest under Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certification for each year from 2000 through 201, areas of forest under Programme for Endorsement of Forest Certification (PEFC) for each year 2000-2014, and areas of forest under domestic forest certification schemes in each year 2000-2012 in its 2015 Global Forest Resources Assessment. Certification programs such as the FSC and PEFC developed in the late 1990s as voluntary tools to promote sustainable forest management and include criteria for best practices to achieve sustainable forest management from environmental, social, and economic perspectives. The data on forests under FSC and PEFC certification were obtained directly from the organizations themselves, while the data on domestic forest certification schemes were collected from individual countries through a survey disseminated to 168 officially nominated national correspondents.
