### Overview The global land use and land cover maps were created by the Global Land Analysis and Discovery Lab (GLAD) laboratory, and the data is available at 30 m spatial resolution for 2000 and 2020. The GLAD laboratory used the spatiotemporally consistent [Landsat Analysis Ready Data (GLAD ARD)](https://glad.umd.edu/ard) to quantify changes in forest extent and height, cropland, built-up lands, surface water, and perennial snow and ice extent over the twenty year period. Each thematic product was independently derived using state-of-the-art, locally and regionally calibrated machine learning tools. The dataset was validated using a statistical sampling which confirms its high accuracy. The Global Land Analysis and Discovery Lab (GLAD) laboratory in the Department of Geographical Sciences at UMD investigates methods, causes, and impacts of global land surface change. Earth observation imagery is the primary data source, and the land cover extent and change is the primary topic of interest. GLAD aspires to generate new science insights concerning land resources, educate the next generation of remote sensing-based land change scientists, and disseminate land monitoring capabilities to operational settings nationally and internationally. ### Methodology The Global Land Analysis and Discovery (GLAD) laboratory derived most global thematic products, except open water, using consistently processed [Landsat Analysis Ready Data (GLAD ARD)](https://glad.umd.edu/ard). The annual GLAD ARD data time series were integrated into a set of phenological metrics that enabled global model calibration and application. The water mapping was performed using the Landsat data processed in the Google Earth Engine using an approach similar to the GLAD ARD. GLAD used a separate supervised classification model to map each thematic class. The decision tree models calibrated with manually collected training data were implemented for water, cropland, and perennial snow and ice mapping. Forest height was estimated using the regression tree model calibrated with Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation Lidar (GEDI) forest structure measurements. The built-up lands were mapped using a deep learning convolutional neural network (CNN) algorithm trained using Open Street Map (OSM) data. The models were calibrated locally (for forest height and cropland mapping) or regionally (all other products). GLAD independently validated each global thematic product using statistical sample analysis. The sample reference data were collected through visual image interpretation using the best available high-resolution satellite data and Landsat time series. The GLAD ARD product consists of 16-day global Landsat normalized surface reflectance and brightness temperature composites combined from the best quality observations. Each 16-day composite includes the normalized surface reflectance for visible, near-infrared, and shortwave infrared Landsat bands and brightness temperature, along with the data quality layer. GLAD integrated the annual GLAD ARD 16-day clear-sky time series into a set of rank-based statistics, hereafter named phenology metrics, that enabled the application of the multitemporal classification and regression models. GLAD augmented the Landsat reflectance metrics with topographic metrics, including elevation and slope. GLAD defined forest as wildland, managed, and planted tree cover, including agroforestry and orchards. The forest extent was defined as an area with tree cover ≥ 5 m, to ensure consistency with the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) forest definition. Nevertheless, their forest definition differs from the one used by the FAO by the inclusion of trees outside forests (agroforestry, orchards, parks) and the exclusion of temporally unstocked forest areas. GLAD employed the global Landsat-based forest height model calibrated for the year 2019 using GEDI observations. For the boreal forests north of 52°N, where GEDI data are absent, GLAD used a regional model approach. Three separate models were calibrated for North America, Europe, and Northern Asia. The model calibrated for the year 2019 was applied to 2000, 2001, 2003, 2017, 2019, and 2020 annual metrics.The forest height values for the years 2000 and 2020 were calculated as the median of 2000, 2001, 2003, and 2017, 2019, 2020 products, respectively, unless forest loss for the years 2001-2003 or 2017-2020 was indicated by the forest disturbance data (in such case, only the year 2000 or 2020 product value was used, respectively). GLAD produced the year 2000 and 2020 forest extent maps by attributing pixels with ≥ 5 m forest height as the “forest” land cover class. The forest extent change (net forest extent loss and gain) was derived directly from the year 2000 and 2020 map comparison. Cropland was defined as land used to produce annual and perennial herbaceous crops for human consumption, forage, and biofuel. The definition excludes tree crops, permanent pastures, and shifting cultivation. Consistent with the FAO arable land category, the fallow length was limited to four years for the cropland class. The cropland mapping was performed for two four-year epochs, 2000-2003 and 2016-2019. For each epoch, they attributed a GLAD ARD pixel as cropland if a growing crop was detected during any year within the interval. The cropland mapping model was calibrated with manually delineated training areas which were extrapolated in space and time through a three-stage algorithm. Supervised classification (bagged decision tree ensembles) was implemented at each of these three steps. The final products were filtered by removing artifacts and cropland patches smaller than 0.5 ha. Built-up land consists of man-made land surfaces associated with infrastructure, commercial and residential land uses. At the Landsat spatial resolution, GLAD defined the built-up land class as pixels that include man-made surfaces, even if such surfaces do not dominate within the pixel. Due to the contextual nature of built-up lands, particularly settlements, they employed a deep learning convolutional neural network (CNN) algorithm to map this thematic class. Final 2000 and 2020 per-pixel class presence probabilities were generated, and validation data were used to assist in the final thresholding of the layers in depicting 2000 and 2020 extents and 2000-2020 gain in built-up lands. Loss of built-up lands, which represents a small proportion of the year 2000 class area, was not mapped by this provisional product. Open surface water, or simply water, is defined as inland water that covers ≥ 50% of a pixel and is not obscured by objects above the surface.The presented multidecadal surface water change product is based on the annual water presence dataset produced by Pickens et al. (2020). Water presence is a percent of Landsat observations classified as surface water of all annual clear-sky observations calculated per pixel. Instead of the GLAD ARD, the algorithm employed the original Collection 1 Tier 1 Landsat 5, 7, and 8 scenes from 1999-2020. GLAD classified each Landsat scene into the land, water, and unusable data classes using an ensemble of hierarchical, bagged classification trees developed for ARD data processing. The perennial snow and ice layer includes land covered by glaciers and snow which remains during the entire year. The map is limited to the GLAD ARD tiles where perennial snow and ice areas were detected using the ARD observation quality layer. GLAD mapped permanent snow and ice using regionally calibrated supervised classification models (decision tree ensembles). Overall, they used fourteen models, one model per mountain system or a geographic region. Each classification model was calibrated with manually collected training data from multitemporal Landsat metrics. Wetlands are treated as a landform containing multiple land cover classes. Topographical metrics, including slope, curvature, and a series of relative elevation layers from variably sized catchments were used to determine wetland versus terra firma. Percent bare ground was included from a previous assessment. GLAD validated each thematic product separately using an independently collected reference data sample. GLAD used different strata designs for each thematic product to target not only the LCLU class of interest but also the potential class omission errors. For product validation, the map and reference data were presented as discrete LCLU classes. The map accuracy metrics include overall accuracy (the proportion of correctly mapped sample pixels), user’s accuracy of the LCLU class (which reflects the thematic class commission), and producer’s accuracy of the LCLU class (which reflects the thematic class omission). Map accuracy statistics were accompanied by the standard error of the estimate (s.e.). We also estimated sample-based areas of LCLU classes and changes with the corresponding s.e. The global composite maps were created by layering an annual vegetation fraction layer with the bare land, wetland landform, followed by the superseding classes of ice, water, cropland, and built-up. The 2019 global composite map can be viewed and downloaded [here](https://glad.umd.edu/dataset/global-land-cover-land-use-v1). For the full documentation of the [landform classes](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/ac46ec) and other [thematic classes](https://doi.org/10.3389/frsen.2022.856903), please see the original methodology. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows datasets from the GLAD laboratory for [Cropland Extent](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/50634b51-ea2e-4cc1-9e4b-8f26a389a301), [Cropland Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ec282483-4f5c-4fb8-ace7-8e557826781a), [Tree Height Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/64a3e126-000b-46fb-aaf4-8ac765a8263b), [Water Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b83ad197-eb95-44e2-8ec3-3351ab926421), [Snow/Ice Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5a796ce9-71d4-42b0-922d-056a86e5eb72), and [Built-Up Area Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e6a3f803-1222-46c2-8e6c-0ae94b3d80c8). _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c37b0b21-3d11-46ea-ba5d-4be4c0caa8ae) as a replacement.**_ ### Overview The Global Hunger Indices show the state of hunger worldwide in 2019, along with three reference years in 2000, 2005, and 2010. The indices capture the multidimensional nature of hunger by calculating Global Hunger Index (GHI) scores comprised of four indicators: undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality. The 2019 Global Hunger Index is published jointly by Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe to measure and track hunger and to spotlight areas with the greatest need to eliminate hunger. The GHI scores are calculated on a 0-100 scale, where 0 indicates no hunger and 100 demonstrates complete hunger. A high GHI score, broadly speaking, can indicate a lack of food, a low-quality diet, insufficient child caregiving practices, an unhealthy environment, or all of these factors. The GHI classifies countries by the following severity layers: low, moderate, serious, alarming, or extremely alarming scales of hunger. ### Methodology GHI scores were calculated using a three-step process that draws on available data from various sources to capture the multidimensional nature of hunger. First, for each country, values were determined for four indicators: 1. Undernourishment: the share of the population that is undernourished (that is, whose caloric intake is insufficient); 2. Child wasting: the share of children under the age of five who are wasted (that is, who have low weight for their height, reflecting acute undernutrition); 3. Child stunting: the share of children under the age of five who are stunted (that is, who have low height for their age, reflecting chronic undernutrition); and 4. Child mortality: the mortality rate of children under the age of five (in part, a reflection of the fatal mix of inadequate nutrition and unhealthy environments). Second, each of the four component indicators was given a standardized score on a 100-point scale based on the highest observed level for the indicator on a global scale in recent decades. Third, standardized scores were aggregated to calculate the GHI score for each country, with each of the three dimensions (inadequate food supply, child mortality, and child undernutrition, which is composed equally of child stunting and child wasting) given equal weight. This three-step process results in GHI scores on a 100-point GHI Severity Scale, where 0 is the best score (no hunger) and 100 is the worst. In practice, neither of these extremes is reached. A value of 0 would mean that a country had no undernourished people in the population, no children younger than five who were wasted or stunted, and no children who died before their fifth birthday. A value of 100 would signify that a country’s undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality levels were each at approximately the highest levels observed worldwide in recent decades. The GHI Severity Scale shows the severity of hunger - from low to extremely alarming - associated with the range of possible GHI scores. ### Overview The Cropland and Pasture Area dataset shows the global distribution of agricultural activities for the year 2000. It is a combination of both satellite based datasets and agricultural inventory data from censuses. The dataset displays the percentage of land used for farming (cropland) and livestock (pasture area) for each grid cell. Each grid cell has a value of 0% to 100% coverage. A value of 0% means there are no agricultural activities present and 100% means the gridcell is completely used for cropland or pasture area. The dataset is displayed at a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes (around 10 kilometers). The Cropland and Pasture Area dataset was created by EarthStat with assistance from the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment (UMN IonE), and the Land Use and Global Environment Lab at the University of British Columbia (LUGE Lab at UBC). It was created to help understand the positive social and economic benefits, as well as the negative environmental consequences, of agricultural land use. ### Methodology The Cropland and Pasture Area in 2000 dataset was created by combining two different high-resolution satellite based land cover datasets and agricultural inventory data. The agricultural inventory data is allocated to the 10 kilometer resolution using the higher resolution land cover datasets and statistical modeling. The two satellite based land cover datasets used were the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Land Cover Type Product and the Satellite Pour l’Observation de la Terre (SPOT) VEGETATION based Global Land Cover 2000 (GLC2000) dataset. The MODIS dataset was created with data collected from October 2000 to October 2001 and was analyzed using remote imaging with a globally consistent classification scheme. The SPOT dataset was created with data from November 1999 to December 2000 and used a variable land use classification scheme that included information from regional institutions. Both datasets have a spatial resolution of about 1 kilometer. A single land cover dataset was created by overlaying the MODIS and GLC2000 datasets, where each classification was the combination of the MODIS and GLC2000 classifications. This combination land cover product was found to provide more accurate results when calibrated against the inventory data, as opposed to using either data set individually. Cropland and pasture inventory data was compiled for the globe at the national and subnational level for circa year 2000. This resulted in compiled data for 15,990 different administrative units of the world, ranging from political units like countries, states and counties. Inventory data was found from either census data or the Food and Agriculture Organization's (FAO) [FAOSTAT database](http://faostat.fao.org). The cropland and pasture data was compiled to be consistent with the FAO definition of “Arable lands and permanent crops” and “Permanent pastures” respectively. The agricultural inventory data were seldom available exactly for the year 2000, therefore the authors collected inventory data between the years 1998 to 2002 where possible, but in several instances relied on older data. Information within the final Cropland and Pasture Area dataset for areas that were clearly non-agricultural (tundra, boreal forest, and protected land) were masked to reduce the possibility of misclassification. For full information, please see the source [methodology](http://www.earthstat.org/cropland-pasture-area-2000/). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

The Land Matrix Online Database on Land Deals tracks large-scale land deals that are made for agricultural production, timber extraction, carbon trading, industry, renewable energy production, conservation, and tourism in low- and middle-income countries. A deal is referred to as an intended, concluded, or failed attempt to acquire land through purchase, lease, or concession that must (1) entail a transfer of rights to use, control, or ownership of land through sale, lease, or concession; (2) have been initiated since the year 2000; (3) cover an area of 200 ha or more; and (4) imply the potential conversion of land from smallholder production, local community use, or important ecosystem service provision to commercial use. Resource Watch shows the number of concluded deals that cover an area of 200 ha or more per year since 2000. Because of the nature of land acquisitions, it is difficult to obtain this information from official sources, therefore data are attained from (1) research papers and policy reports by international and local organizations and NGOs; (2) personal information contributed through the Global Observatory website; (3) field-based research projects; (4) official government records; (5) company websites; and (6) media reports. The Gridded Population of the World, Version 4 (GPW v4), Population Density Adjusted to Match 2015 Revision of UN WPP Country Totals, produced by SEDAC, consists of estimates of human population density, based on counts consistent with national censuses and population registers with respect to relative spatial distribution but adjusted to match the 2015 revision of UN World Population Prospects country totals for the years 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, and 2020. The Climate Resilience Screening Index (CRSI), developed by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), characterizes U.S. county and community resilience based on a suite of indicators that are grouped into broad categories of county and community resiliency traits in the context of natural disasters. The index is a composite measure comprised of five domains (Risk, Governance, Society, Built Environment, and Natural Environment), represented by 20 indicators, and calculated from 117 metrics. CRSI characterizes holistic climate resilience throughout the U.S. at the county level (2000-2015); ascertains the relationships among those domains and indicators; and provides information regarding how that resilience score is constructed and the actions a community/county can take to improve their climate resilience. CRSI is intended to be used by EPA Regions and others who work closely with counties and communities to gauge resilience of built and natural systems to acute climate events (e.g., hurricanes, wildfires, tornadoes, flooding). ### Overview This dataset shows national-level electricity generation from renewable energy technologies between 2000 and 2018. Renewable energy generation measures the amount of electricity actually produced by renewable energy sources. Renewable energy is defined as energy that comes from natural resources that are continually restored. In this dataset, renewable energy sources include wind, solar, hydropower, biofuels, municipal waste, biogas, geothermal, and marine energy. Transitioning to renewable energy technologies can be beneficial to the economy and human health, as well as help reduce climate change. Electricity generation is one of the largest [sources of greenhouse gas emissions](https://www.epa.gov/ghgemissions/sources-greenhouse-gas-emissions), directly contributing to climate change. Transitioning to renewable energy technologies can help reduce our greenhouse gas emissions and be part of the solution to addressing climate change. Renewable energy production also produces less air pollution, which is linked to a number of health concerns, than most fossil fuel energy sources. Furthermore, these technologies provide a reliable source of energy and help diversify energy portfolios, reducing the potential of energy scarcity. This dataset was produced by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) and is updated annually. ### Methodology Data was obtained from a variety of sources, including an IRENA questionnaire, official national statistics, industry association reports, consultant reports and news articles. description: The MODIS Normalized Difference Snow Index (NDSI) snow cover layer, from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), shows the presence of snow cover over land and water bodies as an index related to the presence of snow. NDSI snow cover is derived from the cloud free snow reflectance sensed by the MODIS instrument, and hence this layer shows presence of snow during day time and under cloud clear condition only. NDSI snow cover though could be retrieved in the valid range of (0, 1.0) at every pixel, additional tests like surface temperature screening linked with the surface height is used for accurate detection. Snow is precipitation that forms from water vapor in the atmosphere where temperatures are below 0° Celsius. If the ground temperature is also below freezing, snow will accumulate on the ground as bright, white layer of snowpack. Snow cover reflects sunlight back into the atmosphere, helping to cool the Earth’s surface. Snowmelt is used for drinking water and crop irrigation, and can moisturize soil to reduce the risk of wildfire in many areas in the world. When snow melts in the spring, too much snow can cause springtime flooding. The MODIS Snow Cover (Normalized Difference Snow Index) layer is available from both the Terra (MOD10) and Aqua (MYD10) satellites. The sensor and imagery resolution is 500 m, the geographic coverage is global, and the temporal resolution is daily. Monthly averages for each CMG cell are calculated from the corresponding 28 – 31 days of observations in the MOD10C1 daily maximum snow cover extent data set. The input data are filtered to utilize only the clearest surface views in the average and to remove low magnitude snow cover fractions in the output that likely reflect erroneous snow detections.Algorithm Description Average snow cover is calculated for each cell in the CMG using the 28 – 31 days of MOD10C1 (daily snow cover) for the month. Data is filtered so that the most relevant days of snow cover are used to calculate the average and to filter out data that is of low magnitude i.e. low occurrence of snow during the month. The latter filter works to remove some occurrences of erroneous snow from the monthly snow average. The daily snow data is used to compute the monthly average snow cover. A daily cell must have a Clear Index (CI) of > 70% to be included in the average. Clear index is defined as the number of cells without clouds divided by the total number of cells.That filter is applied so that only the clearest of the daily observations are included in the average. (See the MOD10C1 section for description of the CI.) A daily observation contributes to the monthly average for a cell as follows: Daily contribution to monthly mean = 100 * snow%/CI For daily observations that are cloud free the snow contribution to the mean is the observed snow fraction in a grid cell. For daily observations of mixed snow and cloud fractions with a high CI it is assumed that there is some fraction of snow cover obscured by cloud. In that case the daily snow observation is increased in that equation so that the contribution to the monthly mean will be greater than the daily snow observation. For example, a cell has 25% snow cover and the CI = 75 then the cell is determined to have (25%/75 * 100) = 33% fractional snow cover. Daily observations with a CI ≤ 70 are assigned either as 100% cloudy, night, missing or no decision. There must be at least one day in the month for each cell with the CI > 70 in order for the mean snow cover to be computed for that cell of the monthly CMG. If that restriction is not met then the cell is reported as no decision. A second filter is applied to the calculated mean fractional snow cover of each cell to filter out those cells in which the magnitude of snow cover is less than 10%. Cells failing the filter are assigned 0% snow for the month. Cells with a low magnitude are considered suspect of being erroneous snow originating in the MOD10_L2 algorithm and being propagated through the sequence of snow products. The magnitude of snow is calculated as an average snow for all days with snow passing the first filter of CI > 70. Data displayed on Resource Watch is filtered to only show snow cover greater than 20 percent. description: The Political Violence Risk Assessment dataset was originally published by The Hague Centre for Strategic Studies (HCSS). Its purpose is to forecast the onset of large-scale political violence. Countries are evaluated to determine their "risk" of experiencing a large-scale political violence event in the next month using structural data (infant mortality, regime type, conflicts in neighboring countries, and state-led discrimination) and automated event data (protests, assaults, and expressions of disapproval) from the previous month, which are combined in a logistic regression model. The score is normalized between 0 and 100 and indicates the percentile rank of probability of onset. Infant mortality data are from World Development Indicators; other structural data are from the Center for Systemic Peace; event data are from the Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone; and normalization and aggregation were done by the HCSS. ### Overview The Tree Cover dataset measures areas of tree cover in 2000. Tree cover is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters (m) in height and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. The dataset has a spatial resolution of 1 arc second which is approximately 30 m × 30 m at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Forests provide a wide range of ecosystem services that are [critical to biodiversity richness, climate regulation, carbon storage, and water supplies](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/309/5734/570?ijkey=493d3bb49264119aa5ed9175119f7e221b2093d6&keytype2=tf_ipsecsha). They provide shelter to a variety of wildlife species and supply humans with [essential products including lumber, paper, and firewood]( https://www.fs.fed.us/forestmanagement/products/#:~:text=Forest%20products%20include%20materials%20derived,nuts%2C%20and%20other%20natural%20products). In the global fight against climate change, the forest ecosystem is playing an incredibly important role since it [absorbs and stores large amounts of carbon](https://www.undp.org/content/undp/en/home/blog/2018/Forests-A-natural-solution-to-climate-change-crucial-for-a-sustainable-future.html). Through measuring the tree cover density of global forests, this dataset provides decision makers with a consistent basis on which to understand the [causes of tree cover loss](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/342/6160/850). It also helps to quantify other critical environmental issues, such as the economic drivers of [natural forest conversion to more intensive land uses](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1549-0831.1998.tb00691.x) and the effectiveness of [protected areas around the globe](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02422) to represent species diversity. The dataset was created through a collaboration among the Global Land Analysis & Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland (UMD), Google, United States Geological Survey (USGS), and National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) with the aim to provide a spatially and temporally detailed quantification of global forest change. ### Methodology The data was generated using multispectral satellite imagery from three sources: the Landsat 5 thematic mapper, the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager sensors. [Images captured during growing seasons](https://doi.org/10.14358/PERS.70.3.313) were used since they are more appropriate for mapping land cover. More than 1 million satellite images were processed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval and 400,000 Landsat 5, 7 and 8 images for the 2011-2019 interval. The following steps were taken to pre-process the images: 1. Pixel values were recalculated if image resolutions were changed. 2. Images were screened for clouds, shadows and water. 3. Images were [calibrated and normalized](http://gsp.humboldt.edu/OLM/Courses/GSP_216_Online/lesson4-1/radiometric.html) to make them comparable with one another. Land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled with a supervised learning algorithm, which involved [using labeled data to develop a machine learning model](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/problem-framing/cases#what-is-supervised-learning) to identify per pixel tree cover. To facilitate processing, each continent was characterized individually: North America, South America, Eurasia, Africa, and Australia using [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/), a cloud platform for earth observation data analysis that combines a public data catalog with a large-scale computational facility capable of handling large volumes of geospatial data. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [Tree Cover Loss](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5c5e654e-182b-4ab4-8a3c-edff79cc68ea) and [Tree Cover Gain](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/426fe3f0-12de-4adb-b3aa-850eb04f75b4) from the same dataset. description: The Global Grid of Probabilities of Urban Expansion to 2030 by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center (NASA SEDAC) presents spatially explicit probabilistic forecasts of global urban land cover change from 2000 through 2030 at a 2.5 arc-minute resolution. For each grid cell that is nonurban in 2000, a Monte Carlo model assigned a probability of becoming urban by the year 2030. The authors first extracted urban extent circa 2000 from the NASA MODIS Land Cover Type Product, Version 5, which provides a conservative estimate of global urban land cover. The authors then used population densities from the Global Rural-Urban Mapping Project, Version 1 (GRUMP v1), to create the population density driver map. They estimated the amount of new urban land in each UN region by 2030 in a Monte Carlo fashion based on present empirical distribution of regional urban population densities and probability density functions of projected regional population and GDP values for 2030. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

### Overview Untreated connected wastewater measures the percentage of domestic wastewater that is connected through a sewerage system and not treated to at least a primary treatment level. Higher values indicate higher percentages of point source wastewater discharged without treatment. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low (<30%) to extremely high (>100%). Wastewater discharge without adequate treatment could expose water bodies, the general public, and ecosystems to pollutants such as pathogens and nutrients. The indicator compounds two crucial elements of wastewater management: connection and treatment. Low connection rates reflect households’ lack of access to public sewerage systems; the absence of at least primary treatment reflects a country’s lack of capacity infrastructure, institutional knowledge) to treat wastewater. Together these factors can indicate the level of a country’s current capacity to manage its domestic wastewater through two main pathways: extremely low connection rates (below 1 percent), and high connection rates with little treatment. Values are available per country. ### Methodology Sewerage connection and wastewater treatment data come from a white paper published by the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) and Veolia (Xie et al. 2016). In brief, Xie et al. aggregate three of the leading research papers on country-level connection and treatment rates into one data set through a hierarchical methodology. The data includes the percentage of households connected to sewerage systems (percent connected), and the percentage of wastewater connected left untreated (i.e., not treated using primary, secondary, or tertiary treatments) (percent untreated). The calculation is based on the Yale Environmental Performance Index’s Wastewater Treatment (WWT) indicator [(Wendling et al. 2018)](https://epi.envirocenter.yale.edu/node/36476). WWT examines the performance of wastewater treatment [(Wendling et al. 2018)](https://epi.envirocenter.yale.edu/node/36476). The untreated, connected wastewater indicator reverses the WWT to instead examine the hazard. The first step in the calculation was to group all countries with a household sewage connection rate of less than 1% into the “Low to no wastewater connected” category. For all remaining countries, the percent of wastewater treated to at least primary treatment (100% - percent of untreated wastewater) was calculated. This was multiplied by the household connection rate to find the percent of treated connected wastewater. Next, the percent of treated connected wastewater was subtracted from 100% to find the percent of untreated connected wastewater. Finally, raw untreated connected wastewater values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw untreated connected wastewater values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds. - Low (0-1): < 30% - Low to medium (1-2): 30 - 60% - Medium to high (2-3): 60 - 90% - High (3-4): 90 - 100% - Extremely high (4-5): 100% - Low to no wastewater (5): -1 For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. ### Overview This dataset includes the percentage of people using drinking water from an improved source that is accessible, available when needed, and free from contamination. It provides values for the years 2000 to 2017 for rural populations. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), safely managed drinking water is defined as an improved water source that is accessible on premises, available when needed and free from fecal and priority chemical contamination. Improved water sources include piped water, boreholes or tubewells, protected dug wells, protected springs, and packaged and delivered water. WHO and UNICEF’s Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation, and Hygiene prepared this dataset. Access to safe drinking water is a human right, not a privilege, for everyone. Access to safe water can reduce illness and death from disease, improve health, reduce poverty, and lead to socioeconomic development. Yet many countries still lack access to safe drinking water. Children are especially vulnerable to deaths and illnesses related to lack of access to proper drinking water services. In addition, women and girls are almost two and a half times more likely than men and boys to fetch water, reducing their time for other activities, such as attending school. ### Methodology This dataset was developed based on administrative sources, national censuses, and nationally representative surveys. A weighted average was calculated to aggregate subnational data to the national level. There are three criteria for an improved water source: (1) accessibility: water should be accessible on the premises, (2) availability: water should be available when needed, and (3) quality: water supplied should be free from contamination. The WHO/UNICEF JMP provides national estimates only when data is available on drinking water quality and at least one of the criteria (accessibility and availability). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://databank.worldbank.org/reports.aspx?source=2&type=metadata&series=SH.H2O.SMDW.ZS). ### Additional Information Additional data for the percentage of the population with access to an improved water source at [urban]((https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Access-to-an-Improved-Water-Source-Urban) and [national](https://.resourcewatch.org/data/explore/wat005a-Access-to-an-Improved-Water-Source-National-Level_1) levels is available on Resource Watch. The Malaria Extent dataset is provided by the Malaria Atlas Project (MAP) and shows the estimated proportion of 2-10 year olds in the general population that are infected with P. falciparum at any one time at a global scale. Malaria is a disease caused by parasites that are transmitted to humans by Anopheles mosquitoes. Two related parasite species cause the majority of disease and death from malaria: Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax. In areas affected by malaria, children and pregnant women are especially vulnerable, a condition further compounded by poverty. MAP conducted surveys to collect data on malaria cases. Each survey included in the MAP parasite database has been disaggregated to individual sites (geographical points), individual dates (if the same site was sampled repeatedly), and individual parasite species. Conversely, individual-level survey data have been aggregated up to the community level at a particular site and time. MAP data spans 2000-2017. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. ### Overview The city expansion index dataset shows outward and upward urban growth in 377 cities globally that have a population of over 1 million residents. Outward growth is the horizontal expansion of buildings and upward growth is the vertical expansion of buildings. The final dataset was normalized into comparable values called the Upward Growth Index and Outward Growth Index. A higher expansion index value means more growth is occurring. The dataset uses remote sensing data collected between 2000 and 2014. This dataset was created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) as part of the World Resources Report (WRR) Towards a More Equal City. It is intended to highlight regional trends in urban expansion and differences in urban structure within and between cities. Ultimately, it can be used to help governments understand how urban expansion can be managed in a way that achieves more equitable access to core services for the under-served while bringing wider economic and environmental benefits to cities. For the dataset to paint a complete picture it should ideally be used in conjunction with a matching dataset on the socioeconomic information of the city. ### Methodology This dataset was created using a combination of remote sensing data to determine upward and outward expansion in cities with a metropolitan population greater than 1 million. Remote sensing data was collected from mean summer backscatter power ratio (PR) from NASA's SeaWinds microwave scatterometer (Ku-band, 13.4 GHz) and built-up area from the multitemporal Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL). The data showed the outward growth of urban built-up areas between 2000 and 2014 measured from the Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL) and upward growth between 2001 and 2009 measured using the power ratio (PR) from NASA’s SeaWinds microwave scatterometer. Each dataset was reprocessed to have the same spatial resolution of 0.05 degrees (about 5.6 km at the equator). To determine which cities had a metropolitan population greater than 1 million, Landscan data created by the Oak Ridge National Laboratory was combined with the Oxford Economics database to create a combined dataset of 377 cities. Researchers overlayed an 11x11 pixel grid (121 total pixels) over each city using the dataset Populated Places from Natural Earth to create a unified boundary to measure the cities growth. The 11x11 grids were extracted and all grid cells with a built up value less than 20 percent were masked in GHSL. Total upward and outward growth were then calculated using the remaining pixels for each city by using a cluster analysis to group each pixel into similar urban growth patterns and structures. Finally, the values were converted into the upward urban growth index and outward urban growth index to allow for comparison of the values across cities. The final dataset was presented in raster format at a spatial resolution of 0.28 degrees (20.98 square kilometers at the equator). description: The Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) collects and prepares satellite and ground-based observation data products for use in Land Surface Models (LSMs). These data are a result of forcing the National Centers for Environmental Prediction / Oregon State University / Air Force / Hydrologic Research Lab (NOAH) LSM. The GLDAS is developed and distributed by NASA and the Goddard Earth Sciences Data and Information Services Center (GES DISC). GLDAS 2.1 data are available in 3-hour and monthly increments, covering the years from 2000 to near-present. This selection of GLDAS contains data on the amount of water stored as root-level soil moisture. The GLDAS incorporates satellite data on vegetation derived from the Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR), soil parameter maps, and topographic maps. **CONSULT EXPERTS TO FINISH** , https://hydro1.gesdisc.eosdis.nasa.gov/data/GLDAS/GLDAS_NOAH025_3H.2.0/doc/README_GLDAS2.pdf

Increases in the rates of hospital admission for heat stress are one potential impact of rising global temperatures. Tracking Crude Rate of Hospitalization for Heat Stress per 100,000 Population can help document changes over place and time, monitor vulnerable areas, and evaluate the results of local climate-adaptation strategies. Heat stress can manifest in a number of clinical outcomes, and people with chronic health problems (e.g., cardiovascular disease, diabetes, obesity) are more susceptible to the effects of heat than healthy individuals. For these reasons, heat stress may not be listed as the primary diagnosis. This indicator therefore includes all cases where heat stress is explicitly listed as the primary diagnosis or any other diagnosis. The hospital data shown here are provided by state and/or local public health departments to the National Environmental Public Health Tracking Program. Data are based on the date of admission rather than the date of discharge. For these measures, admission date is limited to between May 1 and September 30 for each year. These data represent number of admissions rather than number of individuals admitted to the hospital. The Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Tracking Network suppresses data for counties with non-zero counts less than 6 and population less than 100,000 to protect confidentiality. This data set covers the United States from 2000 to 2016. Data on states designated as 'unstable', or counties corresponding with relative standard error greater than 30%, have been excluded in this visualization. See the original data source for this information.

_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c37b0b21-3d11-46ea-ba5d-4be4c0caa8ae) as a replacement.**_ ### Overview The Global Hunger Indices show the state of hunger worldwide in 2018, along with three reference years in 2000, 2005, and 2010. The indices capture the multidimensional nature of hunger by calculating Global Hunger Index (GHI) scores comprised of four indicators: undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality. The 2018 Global Hunger Index is published jointly by Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe to measure and track hunger and to spotlight areas with the greatest need to eliminate hunger. The GHI scores are calculated on a 0-100 scale, where 0 indicates no hunger and 100 demonstrates complete hunger. A high GHI score, broadly speaking, can indicate a lack of food, a low-quality diet, insufficient child caregiving practices, an unhealthy environment, or all of these factors. In the GHI by Severity layers, countries are classified as having low, moderate, serious, alarming, or extremely alarming scales of hunger. ### Methodology GHI scores were calculated using a three-step process that draws on available data from various sources to capture the multidimensional nature of hunger. First, for each country, values were determined for four indicators: 1. Undernourishment: the share of the population that is undernourished (that is, whose caloric intake is insufficient); 2. Child wasting: the share of children under the age of five who are wasted (that is, who have low weight for their height, reflecting acute undernutrition); 3. Child stunting: the share of children under the age of five who are stunted (that is, who have low height for their age, reflecting chronic undernutrition); and 4. Child Mortality: the mortality rate of children under the age of five (in part, a reflection of the fatal mix of inadequate nutrition and unhealthy environments). Second, each of the four component indicators was given a standardized score on a 100-point scale based on the highest observed level for the indicator on a global scale in recent decades. Third, standardized scores were aggregated to calculate the GHI score for each country, with each of the three dimensions (inadequate food supply, child mortality, and child undernutrition, which is composed equally of child stunting and child wasting) given equal weight. This three-step process results in GHI scores on a 100-point GHI Severity Scale, where 0 is the best score (no hunger) and 100 is the worst. In practice, neither of these extremes is reached. A value of 0 would mean that a country had no undernourished people in the population, no children younger than five who were wasted or stunted, and no children who died before their fifth birthday. A value of 100 would signify that a country’s undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality levels were each at approximately the highest levels observed worldwide in recent decades. The GHI Severity Scale shows the severity of hunger - from low to extremely alarming - associated with the range of possible GHI scores. This data set on deforestation drivers was adapted from Hosonuma et al. (2012) and illustrates the contribution of various industries ("drivers") to deforestation in Africa, the Americas and Asia (including Oceania). The driver data are summarized and analyzed for each of the 3 continents. Agriculture is the main driver of deforestation, but with geographic differences in the importance of commercial versus subsistence agriculture. The data include continental-level estimations for the relative area proportion and absolute net forest area change in km2 yr−1 (FAO 2010) for the period 2000–2010, deforestation drivers, and the relative disturbed forest area fraction of degradation drivers. The estimates are based on data from 46 tropical and subtropical countries and were obtained by the authors from REDD+ reports as well as Center for International Forestry Research country profiles (which include driver and activity information for deforestation and forest degradation), United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change National Communications, and other reports. In total, driver data were available for 46 of the 100 (sub)tropical non-Annex I countries. These 46 countries account for 78% of the total forest area (in 2010) and 81% of forest loss (in 2000–2010) of the 100 countries under consideration, according to 2010 data from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization Forest Resources Assessment (FAO 2010), and cover a range of forest transition (FT) phases on each continent. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. ### Overview The Burned Areas dataset shows areas that have experienced fire events in near real-time. The dataset provides the approximate date in which the burning occurred for each of the 500 meter (m) grid cells. Data is available starting in November 2000 and is updated on a monthly basis. [According to the United States Geological Survey (USGS)](https://www.usgs.gov/land-resources/nli/landsat/landsat-burned-area?qt-science_support_page_related_con=0#qt-science_support_page_related_con), data on burned areas is needed to characterize drivers of fire occurrence, project future fire behavior, and help with assessments of fire impacts on both natural and social systems. The dataset was created by the USGS using satellite imagery. The final product has a resolution of 500 m. ### Methodology The Burned Areas dataset was produced and is continually updated by combining data from both 500 m Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Surface Reflectance imagery and 1 kilometer (km) MODIS active fire observations. This hybrid algorithm uses a burn-sensitive vegetation index derived from MODIS short-wave infrared bands 5 and 7. In addition, the active fire maps are used to guide the selection of burned and unburned training samples. If a grid cell has been marked as burned, the dataset identifies the date when the burn occurred within that cell. The dataset also includes special values for missing data, unburned cells, and water grid cells. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/documents/114/MCD64_User_Guide_V6.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional information on the uncertainty of burn date data, quality assurance indicators, and the first and last days of the burn for each burned area can be found in the original source data. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. The original dataset contained burned, unburned, and water grid cells. Only burned area grid cells are displayed on Resource Watch. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

### Overview The Global Cropland Extent dataset at 30 m spatial resolution was developed by the Global Land Analysis and Discovery Lab (GLAD) at the University of Maryland (UMD) using Landsat satellite data time-series. Cropland is defined as land used to produce herbaceous crops for human consumption, forage, and biofuel. Perennial woody crops, permanent pastures, and shifting cultivation are excluded from the definition. The map is based on the machine learning classification of the global Landsat data archive using locally calibrated models. Model calibration data were collected through visual interpretation of Landsat and high spatial resolution satellite images. The mapping was performed for 2000-2003, 2004-2007, 2008-2011, 2012-2015, and 2016-2019 time intervals. For each four-year interval, a 30x30 m pixel was mapped as cropland if a growing crop was detected during any of these years. **Cropland change data are available**[here](https://bit.ly/34QydNx). Global population growth and increasing standards of living inevitably cause the expansion and intensification of global agricultural land use to fulfill growing demands for food, biofuel, and other commodities. In turn, agriculture expansion and intensification threaten ecosystem functioning and lead to species extinction through habitat loss and fragmentation. The [United Nations 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)](https://www.undp.org/sustainable-development-goals) call for balancing increasing agricultural production with maintenance of ecosystem services. Implementation of SDGs to improve food security, protect freshwater and terrestrial ecosystems, and mitigate climate change require national policies and international cooperation that are based on consistent, independent, and timely data on agriculture extent and productivity. The Cropland Extent and Change dataset can serve as a tool for monitoring national and global progress towards SDGs. The GLAD laboratory in the Department of Geographical Sciences at UMD investigates methods, causes, and impacts of global land surface change. Earth observation imagery is the primary data source and land cover extent and change is the primary topic of interest. GLAD aspires to generate new science insights concerning land resources, educate the next generation of remote sensing-based land change scientists, and disseminate land monitoring capabilities to operational settings nationally and internationally. ### Methodology Cropland is defined as land used for the production of annual and perennial herbaceous crops for human consumption, forage (including hay), and biofuel. Perennial woody crops, permanent pastures, and shifting cultivation are excluded from the definition. The fallow length is limited to four years for the cropland class. The cropland class definition is largely consistent with the arable land category reported by the [Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations](https://www.fao.org/3/Y4171E/Y4171E20.htm). The analysis was performed in four-year epochs, 2000-2003, 2004-2007, 2008-2011, 2012-2015, and 2016-2019. One cropland map per epoch was created. Using a four-year interval (rather than a single year) increased the number of clear-sky satellite observations in the time-series, which improves the representation of land surface phenology and the accuracy of cropland detection. For each four-year interval, an area was mapped as cropland if a growing crop was detected during any of these years. This way, the criterion of the maximum fallow length was implemented: if an area was not used as cropland for more than four years, it was not included in the cropland map for the corresponding time interval. The global 16-day normalized surface reflectance Landsat Analysis Ready Data (Landsat ARD) was employed as input data for cropland mapping [(Potapov et al., 2020)](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/12/3/426). For each four-year interval, a single annualized gap-free 16-day observation time-series was created. For each 16-day interval, the observation with the highest near-infrared reflectance value was selected (to prioritize observations with the highest vegetation cover) from four years of Landsat data. The annualized 16-day time series within each four-year interval was transformed into a set of multitemporal metrics that provide consistent land surface phenology inputs for global cropland mapping. The Landsat metrics were augmented with elevation data. Global cropland mapping included three stages that enabled extrapolation of visually delineated cropland training data to a temporally consistent global cropland map time-series using machine learning. At all three stages, bagged decision tree ensembles were employed as a supervised classification algorithm that uses class presence and absence data as the dependent variable and a set of multitemporal metrics as independent variables at a Landsat ARD pixel scale. The first stage consisted of performing individual cropland classifications for a set of 924 Landsat ARD 1°×1° tiles for the 2016-2019 interval. At the second stage, the 924 tiles that had been classified as cropland/other land and the 2016-2019 metric set were used to train a series of regional cropland mapping models. At the third stage, the preliminary global cropland maps were used as training data to generate temporally consistent global cropland data. The goal of this third stage was to create a robust spatiotemporally consistent set of locally calibrated cropland detection models. For each 1°×1° Landsat ARD tile (13,451 tiles total) training data for each four-year interval was collected from the preliminary cropland extent maps within a 3° radius of the target tile, with preference to select stable cropland and non-cropland pixels as training. Training data from all intervals were used to calibrate a single decision tree ensemble for each ARD tile. The per-tile models were then applied to each time interval, and the results were post-processed to remove single cropland class detections and omissions within time-series and eliminate cropland patches below 0.5 ha. Manual masks to remove map artifacts (e.g., cropland overestimation over temperate wetlands and flooded grasslands) were applied in some regions to improve the final map. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows datasets from the GLAD laboratory for [Cropland Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ec282483-4f5c-4fb8-ace7-8e557826781a), [Tree Height Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/64a3e126-000b-46fb-aaf4-8ac765a8263b), [Water Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b83ad197-eb95-44e2-8ec3-3351ab926421), [Snow/Ice Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5a796ce9-71d4-42b0-922d-056a86e5eb72), [Built-Up Area Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e6a3f803-1222-46c2-8e6c-0ae94b3d80c8), and [Land Cover Map](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/06e734af-66f0-4c3e-ac71-1b99f3cbfe1d). ### Overview The Snow/Ice Change dataset at 30 m spatial resolution was developed by the Global Land Analysis and Discovery Lab (GLAD) at the University of Maryland (UMD) using Landsat satellite data time-series. The map shows the extent of glaciers and perennial snowfields and their net change from the year 2000 to 2020. Areas with seasonal snow cover are excluded from the map. The map extent is limited to continents and large islands between 75°N and 56°S. Greenland, the Antarctic, and Arctic Islands are excluded from the map. Model calibration data were collected through the visual interpretation of Landsat and high spatial resolution satellite images. A set of regionally calibrated models were developed and implemented to map perennial snow and ice cover time-series. The snow/ice loss represents areas where the year 2000 perennial snow or ice cover was transformed into seasonal snow cover or completely disappeared by the year 2020. The gain areas represent the expansion of perennial snowfields and glaciers from the year 2000 to 2020. The GLAD laboratory in the Department of Geographical Sciences at UMD investigates methods, causes, and impacts of global land surface change. Earth observation imagery is the primary data source, and the land cover extent and change is the primary topic of interest. GLAD aspires to generate new science insights concerning land resources, educate the next generation of remote sensing-based land change scientists, and disseminate land monitoring capabilities to operational settings nationally and internationally. ### Methodology The GLAD laboratory mapped permanent snow and ice using regionally calibrated supervised classification models (decision tree ensembles). The classification model was calibrated with manually collected training data from multitemporal Landsat metrics [(Potapov et al., 2020)](https://doi.org/10.3390/rs12030426). They used the Landsat data from the years 2000, 2005, and 2020 for training data collection. For each year, they selected Landsat observations during the peak land surface temperature and peak vegetation index values to separate perennial and annual snow cover. The training data from different years were integrated and used to create a single regional model. Overall, they created fourteen regional models, one model per mountain system or a geographic region. The models were iterated until the results were sufficiently correct. The final product was filtered using a set of rules to remove noise in the time series and possible omission/commission due to the remaining cloud/cloud shadow contamination of Landsat data. ### Overview The drought risk indicator is based on [Carrão et al. (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gloenvcha.2016.04.012) and was used with minimal alterations. Drought risk was assessed for the period 2000–2014 and is a combination of drought hazard, drought exposure, and drought vulnerability. Higher values indicate higher risk of drought. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low (<0.2) to extremely high (>0.8). Values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6). ### Methodology The methodology for calculating the drought risk indicator was based on [Carrão et al. (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gloenvcha.2016.04.012). Drought hazard was derived from a non-parametric analysis of historical precipitation deficits at the 0.5 degree resolution. Drought exposure was based on a non-parametric aggregation of gridded indicators of population and livestock densities, crop cover and water stress. Drought vulnerability was computed as the arithmetic composite of high level factors of social, economic and infrastructural indicators, collected at both the national and sub-national levels. The hazard, exposure, vulnerability, risk, and no-data mask data available at 5 × 5 arc minute resolution were averaged for each hydrological sub-basin. Finally, raw drought risk values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw drought risk values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds. - Low (0-1): 0.0 - 0.2 - Low to medium (1-2): 0.2 - 0.4 - Medium (2-3): 0.4 - 0.6 - Medium to high (3-4): 0.6 - 0.8 - High (4-5): 0.8 - 1.0 For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. ### Overview The global tree canopy height and change dataset at 30 m spatial resolution was developed through the integration of the [Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI)](https://gedi.umd.edu/) lidar forest structure measurements and [Landsat analysis-ready data (Landsat ARD)](https://www.usgs.gov/core-science-systems/nli/landsat/us-landsat-analysis-ready-data?qt-science_support_page_related_con=0#qt-science_support_page_related_con) time series. The NASA GEDI is a spaceborne lidar instrument operating onboard the International Space Station since April 2019. It provides point-based measurements of vegetation structure, including tree canopy height between 52°N and 52°S globally. The Global Land Analysis and Discover (GLAD) team at the University of Maryland (UMD) integrated the GEDI point-based tree height measurements with the global wall-to-wall Landsat analysis-ready time-series data (Landsat ARD). The GEDI relative height at 95% (GEDI RH95) metric was used to calibrate the model. The Landsat multi-temporal metrics that represent the surface phenology serve as the independent variables for global tree height modeling. The “moving window” locally calibrated and applied regression tree ensemble model was implemented to ensure high quality of tree height prediction and global map consistency. The model was extrapolated in the boreal regions to create the global tree height prototype map. The model was applied for the years 2000 and 2020 and the maps were temporally filtered to provide a two-decade global forest structure and change metrics. The GLAD laboratory in the Department of Geographical Sciences at UMD investigates methods, causes and impacts of global land surface change. Earth observation imagery are the primary data source and land cover extent and change the primary topic of interest. GLAD aspires to generate new science insights concerning land resources, educate the next generation of remote sensing-based land change scientists, and disseminate land monitoring capabilities to operational settings nationally and internationally. ### Methodology The year 2000 and 2020 global tree height was modeled through the integration of the Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) lidar forest structure measurements and Landsat analysis-ready data (Landsat ARD) time-series. The NASA GEDI is a spaceborne lidar instrument operating onboard the International Space Station since April 2019. It provides point-based measurements of vegetation structure between 52°N and 52°S globally [(Dubayah et al., 2020)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666017220300018). The GEDI relative height of returned energy (RH) metrics were filtered to exclude low quality observations and gridded to the Landsat 30-m spatial resolution. The RH metrics were compared with 90th percentile of the tree height at 30-m pixel resolution derived from the airborne lidar instruments and found that the GEDI RH95 (relative height at 95%) metric is highly correlated with the airborne lidar canopy height product. This metric was selected as the calibration data for the global tree height map. To exclude non-woody vegetation from the training, a zero height was assigned to all GEDI observations with RH95 values below 3 meters. A global 16-day normalized surface reflectance Landsat ARD was employed as input data for tree height modeling [(Potapov et al., 2020)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0034425720305381?via%3Dihub). The per-pixel 16-day time-series data were composed only of clear-sky observations during the snow-free season. A set of annual multitemporal metrics was generated to provide consistent land surface phenology inputs for model application. To facilitate spatiotemporal consistency of the reflectance time-series, gap-filling of the missing 16-day data with data from preceding years was implemented. Annual metrics include selected ranks, inter-rank averages, and amplitudes of surface reflectance and vegetation indices values, and surface reflectance averages for land surface phenology stages defined by vegetation indices (i.e., surface reflectance for the maximum and minimum greenness periods). The Landsat metrics were augmented with elevation data. The 2019 GEDI RH95 was used as a dependent variable and the Landsat multitemporal metrics from the same year as independent variables to calibrate the regression tree ensembles. A separate model was calibrated for each Landsat ARD tile (1×1°) using training data collected within the neighboring tiles. The prototype for the boreal tree height map, where GEDI data were absent (north of 52°N), was calibrated using training data extracted from the modeled tree height between 40°N and 52°N. To address the overestimation of tree height over wetlands and tundra, additional non-forest training was manually collected in areas indicated as treeless by the year 2010 tree canopy cover product [(Hansen et al., 2013)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24233722/). The model calibrated for the year 2019 was applied to the multitemporal metrics for other years (2000-2003 and 2017-2020). The tree height value for the years 2000 and 2020 was calculated as the median of 2000, 2001, 2003 and 2017, 2019, 2020, respectively, unless forest loss was indicated by the forest change product [(Hansen et al., 2013)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24233722/). To reduce errors and noise in the model outputs due to remaining atmospheric contamination and differences in the radiometric resolution of Landsat sensors in 2000 and 2020, extensive filtering of the output products was implemented. Pixels that did not experience forest loss according to the Hansen et al. (2013) product and that had an overlap of ranges of tree height values for 2000-2003 and 2017-2020 intervals were considered stable forests. Manual masks were also used to clean up incorrectly mapped forest loss and gain, especially in the short seasonal forests. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows datasets from the GLAD laboratory for [Cropland Extent](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/50634b51-ea2e-4cc1-9e4b-8f26a389a301), [Cropland Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ec282483-4f5c-4fb8-ace7-8e557826781a), [Water Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b83ad197-eb95-44e2-8ec3-3351ab926421), [Snow/Ice Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5a796ce9-71d4-42b0-922d-056a86e5eb72), [Built-Up Area Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e6a3f803-1222-46c2-8e6c-0ae94b3d80c8), and [Land Cover Map](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/06e734af-66f0-4c3e-ac71-1b99f3cbfe1d). The Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Croplands data set was created by EarthStat, University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment and the Land Use and Global Environment Lab at the University of British Columbia and shows greenhouse gas emissions from croplands in the year 2000 for 172 crops. Stabilizing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from croplands as agricultural demand grows is a critical component of climate change mitigation. Emissions intensity metrics---including carbon dioxide equivalent emissions per kilocalorie produced ("production intensity")---can highlight regions, management practices and crops as potential foci for mitigation. Yet their spatial and crop-wise distribution has been uncertain. Here, EarthStat develops global crop-specific estimates of GHG emissions and GHG intensity, circa 2000, in high spatial detail. This includes the effects of rice paddy management, peatland draining and nitrogen (N) fertilizer on methane, carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide emissions. Findings show that current total GHG emissions are largely unrelated to production intensity across crops and countries. Climate mitigation policies should therefore be directed to locations where crops have both high emissions and high intensities. EarthStat calculated GHG emissions from global croplands circa year 2000 for 172 crops. The croplands used in the analysis were derived by distributing agricultural census data onto remotely sensed cropland locations at five arc minute resolution and represent 1997-2003 means of yields and harvested areas. They converted all GHGs to carbon dioxide equivalent using IPCC AR5 100-year global warming potential (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change 5th Report). ### Overview This dataset represents climate model projections of the year in which severe coral bleaching conditions will begin occurring twice per decade and ten times per decade (i.e., annually). The 4 kilometer (km) resolution projections are global, running from 2000 through 2100. Coral communities will start to change when bleaching becomes more frequent than twice per decade: corals susceptible to bleaching will be less common and the structural complexity of many coral reefs will decline. These changes will occur even more rapidly when bleaching events begin to occur annually. These projections are based on future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) 8.5. The RCP 8.5 scenario presumes no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. More information on these scenarios can be found [here](http://tntcat.iiasa.ac.at:8787/RcpDb/dsd?Action=htmlpage&page=about). Mass coral bleaching events due to unusually warm ocean water have increased in frequency and severity, and have become one of the most significant contributors to the deterioration of the world's coral reefs. Furthermore, bleaching events are expected to become more frequent and more severe in the decades ahead. Thermal stress that persists for several weeks with ambient water temperatures as little as 1 to 2 °C above a coral’s thermal tolerance level has been shown to cause bleaching, often on broad geographical scales. Corals can die if thermal stress is severe or long-lasting or if it leads to disease in the colony. Extensive bleaching events have dramatic long-term ecological and social impacts, including loss of reef-building corals, changes in benthic habitat, changes in associated fish populations and economic loss. Even under favorable conditions, it can take decades for severely bleached reefs to fully recover. As the climate continues to warm, bleaching is a major threat to the future of coral reefs. There is great variation in the projected timing of when severe bleaching conditions will become an annual occurrence in most coral reef regions. These large variations can even be seen within a single country’s coral reefs. Reefs projected to experience annual severe bleaching 10 or more years later than other reefs in the same country or territory are considered to be relative refugia: they may provide refuge for aquatic creatures living in surrounding areas with higher levels of bleaching. These relative refugia should therefore be conservation priorities. The projected timing of annual severe bleaching varies by 10 or more years in 71 of the 87 countries and territories with at least 500 square kilometers of reef area. This suggests that these projections should be taken into consideration in most reef areas during conservation and management planning. Coral reefs are among the most biologically rich and productive ecosystems on earth and provide valuable ecosystem benefits to millions of people in coastal areas. They are, however, widely threatened by both local threats (such as overfishing, pollution, and direct physical damage) and the global threats of ocean warming and acidification. These have already caused widespread damage to most of the world’s coral reefs, resulting in reduced areas of living coral, increased algal cover, diminished species diversity, and lower fish abundance, as well as degraded economic and social benefits to many coastal communities. ### Methodology Ensembles of climate models were used to generate projections of the year when severe coral bleaching events will start to occur annually, and of changes in aragonite saturation state. The models were used to generate projected monthly data for the following variables: sea surface temperature (SST), surface pressure of carbon dioxide (CO₂), pH, and salinity. Each model independently generated monthly data for the listed variables, and these model outputs were then adjusted to the mean (within the annual cycle) of observations of SST based on the [OISST V2 1982‐2005 climatology](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/oisst/optimum-interpolation-sea-surface-temperature-oisst-v20). The sea water temperature stress that triggers bleaching is measured in degree heating weeks (DHWs). One degree heating week is equal to one degree above the long-term average summer maximum temperatures for one week. Severe bleaching is common when thermal stress exceeds 8 DHWs. Both bleaching frequency projections have been produced for emissions scenarios RCP8.5 and RCP4.5 (for a total of four projections). RCP8.5 is a "business-as-usual" scenario that assumes emissions increase unabated. At time of dataset production in May of 2016, emissions concentrations were greater than what RCP8.5 had projected for 2016. RCP4.5 assumes emissions stabilize just after 2100 due to successful implementation of climate policies that reduce emissions. These projections are unique in that they have been produced through statistical downscaling so have high resolution (4km) relative to raw climate model data (~1x1°), i.e. relative to the projections [here](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/climate/projections/piccc_oa_and_bleaching/index.php). The final outputs represent the ensemble average, with 33 climate models from the [Coupled Model Intercomparison Project, Phase 5 (CMIP5)](https://pcmdi.llnl.gov/mips/cmip5/) of the [International Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)](http://www.ipcc.ch/) used for RCP8.5 and 35 used for RCP4.5. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only the subset of the dataset corresponding to severe bleaching under the RCP 8.5 scenario. The full dataset includes equivalent data layers about the onset of 2x and 10x per decade bleaching under the RCP 4.5 scenario. Projection results are available in the form of Google Earth files, map images, and ArcGIS-compatible spatial data. The projections can also be viewed on [the UNEPLive site](http://uneplive.unep.org/) under the Coral Reefs theme. The [About page](http://uneplive.unep.org/theme/index/19#about) on UNEPLive also describes the main findings of the research project and discusses the conservation, management and policy applications of the downscaled projections. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch.
